name: Accessible Kazakhstan
description: It is a model of an online map with information on accessibility of public facilities that enables people with limited mobility to navigate the public space.

sdgRelevance.11: The 'Accessible Kazakhstan' map reflects the needs of those who particularly seek accessible, safe and comfortable public space, including people with disabilities, parents with small children in prams, the elderly, pregnant women, temporarily injured people and children under seven years old.  When monitoring a public facility, the owner of the facility is present, and the project team immediately notifies him or her of which elements of the facility do not meet the standards for accessibility of facilities open to the public. On the portal “Accessible Kazakhstan” one can find checklists with criteria for assessing accessibility of facilities, so that, if desired, the owners can read them and afterwards be involved in monitoring independently. Upon request, the project team develops recommendations, on the basis of which owners and government agencies start working on the adaptation of particular facilities for the aforementioned categories of citizens. Based on current data on accessibility of public facilities, comprehensive policies and plans for inclusion can be adopted and implemented. This, in turn, will reduce inequalities and accelerate achievement of other Sustainable Development Goals that affect development of an inclusive society. The world community needs qualified specialists who are able to form a barrier-free environment. It is for the purpose of training such specialists in 2019 within the framework of the “Accessible Kazakhstan” project that a unique online course “Ensuring accessibility of a public facility” was developed. The course: helps to get acquainted with legislation governing the provision of access to public facilities for people with disabilities and other population groups with limited mobility; can be used to find out what criteria accessibility of public facilities and open spaces is evaluated by; explains how to protect one’s right to a barrier-free environment; teaches how to monitor a public facility and develop recommendations for its adaptation to the needs of people with disabilities.

privacyCompliance: The Constitution of the Republic of Kazakhstan, dated 30 August 1995,
The Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan dated 21 May, 2013 № 94-V
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
- Demonstrating the level of accessibility of public facilities, one should take into account that, for example, a person in a wheelchair can not enter a cafe without a ramp, but a person with low vision can. In order to personalize the map for each user, we collect data related to the health conditions of users. Such data is considered particularly sensitive and therefore requires additional protection. To prevent unauthorized access, we use the technical and legal means of data protection described in sections 7 and 9a.
- We also strive to ensure that the information posted on the website is accurate and up-to-date, whether it is a description of accessibility of facilities, or published normative legal acts regarding creation of a barrier-free environment. However, we understand that there is a risk of misinformation due to the fact that occasionally legal acts are amended, and public facilities may eventually be rebuilt, closed or renovated.
 -In this regard, firstly, the administrator of the website monitors the legislation for changes once a month and, if necessary, updates the normative legal acts on the portal of 'Accessible Kazakhstan'.
- Secondly, we have provided for users a function “Confirm data about facility”. If the state of a facility does not match its description on our platform, users can leave feedback and indicate what the discrepancy is. After the administrator gets acquainted with the provided information about the state of the facility, compares the description of accessibility with the provided photos and/ or videos, the updated and / or supplemented version of the facility card will appear in the system. Users can also confirm the description of the facility if they believe that all the information about it is filled in correctly.
 -Thirdly, disclaimers can be found on the platform that we do not give any guarantee regarding the accuracy of information about facilities displayed on the map and we are not responsible for this. We also warn users that normative legal acts are often edited, and we ask the users to check whether the acts remain valid by means of searching them on the information and legal system of normative legal acts of the Republic of Kazakhstan “Adilet” or in the information system “PARAGRAPH”. We collect and use personal data solely for the purposes specified in the privacy policy: to combat spam and protect the users against harassment and hate speech, as well as to keep in touch with the users, in particular to send notifications, requests, responses regarding usage of the portal, provision of services, processing of requests and applications from the users.
We restrict access to personal information to our employees, contractors and agents. Personal data of users is accumulated on the admin panel in the “Users” tab, which only the administrator and programmer have access to. We impose contractual obligations on the administrator: the Agreement on the confidentiality of personal data signed by the administrator states that for violation of confidentiality of personal data, the administrator undertakes to compensate the losses incurred by the subject of personal data in connection with dissemination of personal data, in accordance with the current legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan. Similar agreements will be signed with all employees who have access to personal data of users.
In addition, we employ technical means of data protection (connecting an SSL certificate, using the OAuth2 standard, access right) mentioned in section 7.
We do not allow making user data publicly available and post data about regional coordinators (their names, phones, cities of residence and emails) only with their consent. Additionally, we can destroy the personal data immediately upon the first demand of a user.
contentManagement: Content is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
contentManagementPolicy:
We have developed Community Guidelines that determine what we allow and what we prohibit to post on the website of “Accessible Kazakhstan”.
When a user wants to post information on a new facility on the map, or to supplement or update an existing card (passport) of a facility, all new materials are submitted to the administrator, who, within 24 hours, carefully examines if the information received contains inappropriate or illegal content. During inspection, the administrator checks it against the Community Guidelines, and if requirements for content are violated, it shall not be published.
The portal has a functionality that allows the users to submit a complaint. If a user discovers content that does not comply with the Community guidelines, one can report it in the call center, by mail or by leaving a message in the “Contacts” section. During 24 hours, the administrator analyzes the content against which a complaint was received, and, based on the Community guidelines, determines whether the content is in fact inappropriate. If it is recognized to be inappropriate, the administrator is obliged to remove the content.
harrassmentPolicy: The administrator subjects comments and content to a thorough analysis for compliance with the Community guidelines, and also revises all received complaints regarding content and comments. According to the Community guidelines, if content that violates the rights of minors or that may harm the emotional or physical health of children (representing minors in a sexual context, depicting harmful or dangerous actions involving minors, as well as violence against children and images of a naked child’s body) is detected, it will not be published and comments of this kind will be deleted.,If we think a child is in danger based on reported content, we will assist law enforcement to investigate the violation.,Whenever we become aware of an apparent child sexual abuse, we report it to the “Union of Crisis Centers” on hotline 150 or to the “Emergency Service 111” contact center. The administrator monitors comments on a regular basis. Spam, identical or duplicate comments and comments, the content of which is inappropriate (for a more complete description, see the Community guidelines), shall be deleted. Also, users themselves can submit a complaint about such comments in the manner described above.

name: Accessible Medical Records via Integrated Technologies
description: AMRIT is an open-source platform enhancing primary healthcare by equipping frontline workers with digital tools for data-driven decisions and seamless EHR access through ABDM-compliant, interoperable systems.

sdgRelevance.03: AMRIT directly contributes to SDG 3 by enhancing access to quality primary healthcare through digital tools that empower frontline health workers. By enabling real-time access to Electronic Health Records (EHR), supporting noncommunicable disease management, maternal and child health services, and facilitating telemedicine, AMRIT addresses targets like reducing maternal mortality (3.1), combating communicable and noncommunicable diseases (3.3, 3.4), and achieving universal health coverage (3.8). AMRIT supports SDG 10 by bridging healthcare access gaps for rural and underserved populations. Through features like offline functionality, integration with Mobile Medical Units (MMUs), and multilingual support, AMRIT ensures equitable healthcare delivery, reducing disparities in health outcomes (10.2, 10.3).

ownerName: Piramal Swasthya Management and Research Institute
openAlternatives: AMRIT is designed to be seamlessly integrated with external services and applications. While the platform itself is fully functional and does not depend on closed-source components, integrations with such components as Computer Telephony Interface (CTI) and video conferencing solutions are provided to meet specific project needs. These integrations are implemented on a need basis, including support for Digital Public Goods (DPGs) and other open or closed-source services. AMRIT’s architecture supports modular integrations, ensuring that existing closed-source components can be replaced with open alternatives. For guide on current integrations, refer to: https://piramal-swasthya.gitbook.io/amrit/architecture/integrations The project also uses Google services like Firebase Crashlytics, Firebase Analytics, Firebase Remote Config, Firebase ML Vision, and Google Play Services Nearby Connections. These are used for non-core monitoring and configuration features.
nonPIINotes: AMRIT is a platform used in primary healthcare for managing patient and program data. While it collects some PII data for operational purposes, AMRIT also supports mechanisms for extracting and importing non-PII data in non-proprietary formats for reporting and integration with other systems. AMRIT provides a dedicated reporting database that is optimized for running queries and extracting data without affecting the main operational database. Organizations are encouraged to replicate the main database for reporting and read-heavy queries. Data can be extracted by writing custom SQL queries on the reporting & replication database. Data can be extracted from REST APIs in JSON format if required. AMRIT integrates with systems like DHIS2 for aggregate reporting and dashboarding. More details on data exports and reporting can be found here: https://piramal-swasthya.gitbook.io/amrit/architecture/api-guide https://piramal-swasthya.gitbook.io/amrit/data-management/data-export https://piramal-swasthya.gitbook.io/amrit/data-management/reporting/integrating-dhis2-with-amrit
privacyNotes:
AMRIT complies with relevant privacy and domestic laws that are crucial for the deployment and operation of healthcare platforms in India, including: Information Technology Act, 2000 and corresponding IT Rules 2021: AMRIT adheres to regulations outlined in the Indian IT Act, ensuring compliance with data protection and information security mandates essential for electronic records management. ABDM (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission) Certification: AMRIT has achieved certification under ABDM, confirming that it meets the data privacy, interoperability, and digital health standards established by the Indian government.
Previously, the privacy policy available at https://www.piramalswasthya.org/privacy-policy/ reflected the organization’s overarching guidelines. We have now introduced a dedicated privacy policy specifically for the AMRIT solution, which can be accessed at: https://amrit.piramalswasthya.org/privacy-policy/ This updated policy explicitly references and aligns with the relevant domestic regulations and standards, including Information Technology Act, 2000 and corresponding rules and Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (“DPDP Act”). As AMRIT is typically deployed within state government infrastructure/on-site or secure cloud environments owned by the state, the implementing authority acts as the data controller, and AMRIT functions as the data processor. Accordingly, all compliance with national privacy regulations, including consent, data retention, access management, and security controls, is governed and managed by the data controller.
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
AMRIT follows open-source principles under the GPL-3 license, with all code and documentation publicly available. AMRIT follows a structured SDLC with well-defined stages including requirement gathering, development, implementation, testing, and deployment. Development of the AMRIT platform focuses on understanding the ecosystem, designing with users and building for population scale (https://pmp.piramalswasthya.org/confluence/display/AMRIT/User+Research). Engineering begins with user stories defined in our public JIRA board (https://support.piramalfoundation.org/jira/projects/AMM/issues). All code changes are tracked through GitHub, linked to the JIRA/Scrum board and peer-reviewed. AMRIT uses CI/CD pipelines to ensure coding standards and prevent build failures (https://piramal-swasthya.gitbook.io/amrit/deployment/ci-cd-pipelines). Public roadmap: https://pmp.piramalswasthya.org/confluence/display/AMRIT/AMRIT+Roadmap Release notes: https://pmp.piramalswasthya.org/confluence/display/AMRIT/Release+Notes AMRIT also invites contributions from the open-source community (https://github.com/PSMRI/AMRIT/issues).

Security - HTTPS, SSL, AES. Authentication - JSON Web Tokens. Web standards—AMRIT's web frontend is based on HTML, CSS, and ES6 and communicates with the API backend through RESTful APIs. APIs are documented with the OpenAPI spec and Swagger. In addition, AMRIT is an electronic health record (EHR) platform that supports health standards such as HL7, FHIR, LOINC, and SnomedCT.
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity: AMRIT ensures data privacy and security by implementing industry best practices and robust security measures. The platform is designed with a focus on transparency, data protection, and minimizing risks, ensuring that sensitive healthcare data is safeguarded at all levels. - All data transmitted within the AMRIT platform is encrypted and HTTPS is enforced across all connections - AMRIT employs a hierarchical RBAC system, ensuring that only authorized personnel can access specific data. - All server communications are secured via VPN, and the platform is deployed on hardened servers with firewalls to prevent unauthorized access and mitigate security threats. - Database replication and backups to ensure high availability and reliability. - AMRIT undergoes annual VAPT audits to identify and mitigate potential vulnerabilities, ensuring continuous improvement in security posture. - AMRIT ensures regular updates of libraries and packages to address any identified vulnerabilities promptly, keeping the platform secure and up-to-date. Ref: https://piramal-swasthya.gitbook.io/amrit/data-management/data-privacy-and-security
contentManagement: Content is NOT collected NOT stored and NOT distributed.
harrassmentPolicy: AMRIT is designed exclusively for use by healthcare professionals in clinical and healthcare settings and is not intended for underage users. The software promotes safe and responsible usage, with no elements that could cause harm or restrict user access. For contributors to the AMRIT platform, a Code of Conduct is in place to ensure a positive and respectful collaborative environment. https://github.com/PSMRI/AMRIT/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
otherAdoptingOrganizations: AMRIT has been adopted by multiple government and public health organizations across India: - Sarathi 104 Health Helpline (Assam, India): Operated in collaboration with the State Government of Assam, providing citizens critical health guidance and support. - Medical Health Helpline 104 (Bihar, India): Implemented in partnership with the State Government of Bihar, ensuring accessible healthcare services via teleconsultation. - National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) – 1097 AIDS Helpline (Pan-India): AMRIT powers the nationwide AIDS Helpline (1097), supporting HIV/AIDS awareness, counselling, and assistance across India. - Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) for CSR Projects: AMRIT supports several MMUs deployed under CSR initiatives by companies such as Asian Paints Limited, Shriram Transport Finance Company Ltd (STFC), Sanofi India and Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam (SJVN), India, enabling healthcare services in remote and underserved regions. - Multiple pilot projects for Health and Wellness Centre digitization using the AMRIT Platform in states like Assam, Karnataka and Bihar in partnerships with respective state governments.

name: AGRIS Open Data Set
description: The AGRIS Open Data Set is the Open Data serialization of a big subset of the AGRIS database by FAO, one of the most comprehensive catalogs of food and agricultural scientific literature providing free access to more than 13,000,000 bibliographic records in more than 100 languages.

sdgs.name: SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere

sdgRelevance.01: The AGRIS Open Data Set includes a significant subset (around 50% as of July 2024) of the bibliographic records contributed by the AGRIS network of data providers to the AGRIS database, across all topics in the areas covered by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Sharing publications’ metadata (and in many cases the link to the full text) enhances the reuse of research outputs and knowledge sharing across repositories and institutions, which is essential to make and monitor progress towards the SDGs: in the case of AGRIS, particularly the SDGs that have indicators for which FAO is the custodian UN agency. FAO is the custodian UN agency for 21 indicators and is a contributing agency to 5 more, spanning SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 12, 14 and 15.

ownerName: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
ownershipEvidence: Ownership information is published both on the website (https://www.fao.org/agris/agris-ods) and in the metadata in the datasets at https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dcat/agris (property dc:creator).
redistributionRights: Data providers participating in the AGRIS ODS have declared that they agreed in publishing their data and this information is also available from https://www.fao.org/agris/data-providers, e.g. for the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council (BARC) Open Data Set. This data provider participates in the AGRIS Open Data Set (ODS) https://www.fao.org/agris/data-provider/bangladesh-agricultural-research-council
nonPIINotes: IMPORTING: Bibliographic metadata sets are contributed by the data providers in different ways: they can be harvested via OAI-PMH, or they can be sent by email. Contributed metadata are provided in XML format, and five schemas are accepted: Dublin Core, AGRIS Application Profile (AP), MODS, DOAJ and EndNote. Before publication, metadata are cleaned and normalized in a MongoDB instance, and then exported into an ElasticSearch index. EXTRACTING: Records from data providers agreeing to share their metadata as open data are periodically exported from the index into the XML files which constitute the AGRIS Open Data Set.
privacyNotes:
All FAO applications follow our privacy policy and country-specific applicable laws in accordance with FAO’s rules, policies, and practice, to the exclusion of any single national system of law. 

FAO privacy policy: https://www.fao.org/contact-us/privacy-policy/en, FAO Terms of use: https://www.fao.org/contact-us/terms/en
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
The AGRIS Open Data Set is a collection of datasets extracted from the FAO AGRIS metadata database (https://agris.fao.org/) and made available as XML files using the Dublin Core and the W3C Data Catalog schemas. The solutions adheres to the following open standards: - HTTPS for download: evidence: https://www.fao.org/agris/agris-ods - Standard format: XML: evidence: https://agris.fao.org/ods/AGRIS.ODS.xml Beyond using standard and open protocols and formats, to be fully interoperable, the AGRIS Open Data Set uses well-known and well documented schemas for describing bibliographic resources and datasets: the Dublin Core DCMI Metadata Terms (https://www.dublincore.org/specifications/dublin-core/dcmi-terms/) and the W3C Data Catalog vocabulary (https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat-3/). Evidence: the XML serializations at https://agris.fao.org/ods/AGRIS.ODS.xml can be checked against the relevant schemas (https://purl.org/dc/terms/, https://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/, https://www.w3.org/ns/dcat#). 

AGRIS adheres to the Open Data approach and to and FAIR principles (https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/). --- FAIR principles: - Findable: the datasets and the bibliographic metadata records have unique IDs, which are resolved to URLs using the URI fragment technique. - Accessible: all datasets can be accessed through their URL, and all metadata records can be accessed through their URI fragment identifier using a standardized, open, free communication protocol (HTTP) without authentication. - Interoperable: the metadata is expressed in a formal, accessible, shared, and broadly applicable language for knowledge representation: the XML language, enriched semantically by the use of well-known published schemas (the Dublin Core DCMI Metadata Terms (https://www.dublincore.org/specifications/dublin-core/dcmi-terms/) and the W3C Data Catalog vocabulary (https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat-3/)). - Reusable: Metadata contain a clear and accessible data usage license that permits reuse (dct:license). Metadata are richly described with a plurality of accurate and relevant attributes, defined in the above mentioned schemas.
collectsPII: PII data is NOT collected NOT stored and NOT distributed.
contentManagement: Content is collected stored and distributed.
contentManagementPolicy:
The AGRIS Open Data Set is a collection of metadata describing books, journal articles, monographs, book chapters, datasets and grey literature - including unpublished scientific and technical reports, theses, dissertations and conference papers - in the area of food and agriculture. While the AGRIS website is open to any individual to search or browse the entire collection, this Open Data Set gives access for machine use to a certain number of metadata records (around 50% as of July 2024), which are the records contributed by AGRIS data providers that agree to share the metadata in an open interoperable format. 

The AGRIS Network of data providers are responsible for the content they provide, by having their authorized staff to curate the metadata before submitting it.
otherAdoptingOrganizations:
AGRIS is actively used by the AGRIS Network members that contribute to it, among which Ministries and their libraries constitute 25% of the network. 

Besides governmental, non-governmental and intergovernmental organizations, the AGRIS data providers' network includes research institutions, academia, civil society and publishers among others in more than 150 countries, such as CGIAR centers, CIRAD, Waganingen University, USDA, Kasetsart University, Agency for the Promotion of European Research or Directory of Open Access Journals.

SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals – The Observatory is built upon collaboration with several institutions, including JengaLab, the Central European University, the American University of Central Asia, the Georgian Farmers Association, and the Digital AgriHub.

standardsAndPracticesNotes:
The Agrontology is a standard ontology definition file written in the Ontology Web Language (OWL), openly accessible at a public URI (http://aims.fao.org/aos/agrontology#) resolved to an HTTP URL: http://aims.fao.org/aos/agrontology. The file can be downloaded for local use or used directly by machines at that URL. OPEN PROTOCOLS: a) HTTPS for download: evidence: http://aims.fao.org/aos/agrontology --- OPEN STANDARDS: a) RDF/XML: evidence: http://aims.fao.org/aos/agrontology --- STANDARD LANGUAGES: Beyond using standard and open protocols and formats, to be fully interoperable, the Agrontology is expressed in the RDF "grammar". It uses a standard RDF vocabulary: the Ontology Web Language (OWL), the W3C standard RDF vocabulary to describe ontologies. Evidence: the RDF serializations at http://aims.fao.org/aos/agrontology can be checked against the OWL scheme at http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#.

The Agrontology adheres to the FAIR Principles (https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/) and the Linked Open Data design principles (https://www.w3.org/DesignIssues/LinkedData.html). --- FAIR principles: - Findable: the whole ontology and all properties have unique IDs (URIs) resolved to URLs and publicly available. - Accessible: all (meta)data of the vocabulary are retrievable by their identifier (the URI) using a standardized, open, free communication protocol (HTTP) without authentication. - Interoperable: (Meta)data about the vocabulary and the concepts use a formal, accessible, shared, and broadly applicable language for knowledge representation: the RDF grammar and the Ontology Web Language (OWL), which in turn implements the FAIR principles. - Reusable: (Meta)data are richly described with a plurality of accurate and relevant attributes: the OWL vocabulary is designed to describe ontologies, and in addition the Agrontology uses the Vocabulary of a Friend (VOAF: http://purl.org/vocommons/voaf#) schema and Dublin Core for the metadata. Metadata contain a clear and accessible data usage license. --- Linked Open Data (LOD) design principles: - "Use URIs as names for things": The whole ontology and all properties are identified by URIs resolvable to URLs and publicly available. - "Use HTTP URIs so that people can look up these names": all Agrontology URIs are resolved to URLs. - "When someone looks up a URI, provide useful information, using the standards (RDF, SPARQL)": when looking up a URI, the RDF response is returned. - "Include links to other URIs so that they can discover more things": the Agrontology is not a value vocabulary, so does not include links to other resources, but it reuses URIs from other vocabularies (DCTERMS, OWL, VOAF

description: AGROVOC is a thesaurus of 41,000+ agricultural concepts and relationships in up to 42 languages, available for public use to facilitate access and interoperability of data across institutions and languages. It is maintained by several institutions coordinated by FAO.

sdgs.name: SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere

sdgRelevance.01:
AGROVOC facilitates the exchange and consolidation of knowledge, information, and data in the domains covered by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Consistent use of relevant concepts to index data and resources across repositories and institutions is essential to monitor progress on the SDGs: in the case of AGROVOC, particularly the SDGs that have indicators for which FAO is the custodian UN agency. FAO is the custodian UN agency for 21 indicators and is a contributing agency to 5 more, spanning SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 12, 14, and 15.

Not only does AGROVOC cover all domains related to the SDGs for whose indicators FAO is custodian, but it also includes a dedicated concept for the SDGs and individual sub-concepts for each SDG, with official definitions (https://agrovoc.fao.org/browse/agrovoc/en/page/?uri=http%3A%2F%2Faims.fao.org%2Faos%2Fagrovoc%2Fc_013b16cd).
This helps information and data managers correctly classify resources against the SDGs, and researchers and the general public easily find and browse SDG-related resources and data.

AGROVOC is used to index content and data in many information systems relevant to SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 12, 14, and 15: library catalogs of agriculture/fisheries/nutrition/land research institutions and Ministries, repositories of the CGIAR centers, the FAO AGRIS database and various other FAO resources.

Being a resource managed in partnership with several institutions all over the world, and being coordinated by FAO under the Partnerships and UN Collaboration Division, AGROVOC is particularly relevant to SDG 17.

Code refactoring - Refactoring happens on stories where they are necessary, and cleanup happens when the developer is near the code. All code changes are reviewed. Dependencies are mentioned through package.json or build.gradle, 3. All config is maintained in /etc/ and read through apps, 4. Backing services are declared through config, 5. dataPrivacySecurity:
Privacy
Organisations are encouraged to ask for consent for providing information along with specifying the information being collected, the purpose and information about how it may be used. Many organisations choose to ask and collect consent in audio format. Some provide a text field that they read out and collect consent through an option in their mobile device.

Security
Avni provides options to encrypt data in rest and transit, both within the server as well as in the mobile device. It uses OpenIdConnect (OIDC) for authentication and Role Based Access Control (RBAC) to control access to information to only those who require it.

Avni has gone through a security audit to ensure the app follows OWASP guidelines.
contentManagement: Content is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
contentManagementPolicy:
Avni is used by members of an organisation to record information about beneficiaries. Collected content is usually meant to be used internally and not distributed to anyone outside the organisation. The organisation is the owner of the content.

Most content involves text and numeric fields and multichoice questions. There is the option to add images/videos, which is used by some organisations. The expectation is that the user's contract with its organisation will ensure that inappropriate/illegal content is not stored by the user.

Avni currently does not have mechanisms to identify inappropriate and illegal content, although there are third party mechanisms that can be used to scan and flag content in the object store.
harrassmentPolicy:
Avni is used by members of an organisation to record information about beneficiaries. Direct beneficiary communication is not a core feature of Avni. The organisation is responsible for processes around protection of users and beneficiaries against grief, abuse and harassment. Having said that, there are some features that can help.

1. There is a call masking feature that allows users to call beneficiaries without revealing their phone number. This helps protect users when they are working with a previously unknown group of beneficiaries
2. Avni provides mechanisms to integrate with Glific (an existing DPG), which can be used for two-way communication with beneficiaries. Grievance redressal mechanisms can be implemented on Glific.

name: Bebbo Parenting App
description: Bebbo is an open-source mobile parenting app that empowers parents of 0-6 year-olds with interactive tools to track child development, provides evidence-based insights, stimulating learning activities, and self-care guidance.

sdgRelevance.02: Bebbo promotes SDG 2, 3, 4 and 5. In particular, SDG indicator 2.2.1 (prevalence of childhood stunting), SDG indicator 2.2.2 (prevalence of childhood malnutrition (wasting or overweight)), SDG indicator 3.b.1 (proportion of the target population covered by all vaccines included in their national programme) and SDG indicator 4.2.1 (proportion of children aged 24–59 months (2-5 years) who are developmentally on track in health, learning and psychosocial well-being, by sex). These indicators are supported by providing parents with a rich library of well-researched articles and videos covering various domains of child health. The content is tailored and filtered based on the child's profile, offering personalized recommendations. It covers health and vaccination, early learning protection and safety, nutrition and breastfeeding, and mental health and well-being of parents. The app also includes interactive tools to monitor and support the child's development, optimal growth, and health visits and immunization schedules. By providing accessible information and tools, Bebbo promotes the goal of ensuring a healthy child. In addition, Bebbo has been recognized as a gender transformative initiative by UNICEF. It provides content for fathers and encourages their active involvement in the upbringing of the child. The app promotes increased engagement of both parents in a gender transformative way, supporting the goal of achieving gender equality and empowering all women and girls and hence supports SDG Indicator 5.4.1 (proportion of time spent on unpaid domestic and care work, by sex, age and location).

openAlternatives: The current application is configured to use Google Firebase (and some Facebook SDK APIs) to collect and analyse anonymized usage analytics and for push notifications. name: Cider
description: Cider is a set of software tools for estimating the poverty status of individuals and households using mobile phone data, for use in the targeting and delivery of humanitarian aid.

sdgs.name: SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere

sdgRelevance.01: Cider's purpose is to improve the targeting of humanitarian aid and thereby help alleviate poverty, especially the most extreme poverty. Well-targeted aid is an important tool for poverty reduction in pursuit of SDG 1. As an example, Cider informed the Novissi aid program in Togo, which was carried out jointly by the non-profit GiveDirectly, the Togolese government, and the Global Policy Lab at UC Berkeley. Researchers involved found that Cider's poverty predictions were more accurate than predictions we could have obtained using any viable alternative considered, given the time and resource constraints of the program. This increased accuracy enabled funds to be directed to poorer individuals and households. Details of the program, Cider's role in it, and evaluations of effectiveness can be found in Aiken et al (2022), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04484-9.

ownerName: Regents of the University of California.
nonPIINotes: Cide uses the following open formats: CSV, GeoJSON, YML. As well as a set of standardized data formats (https://global-policy-lab.github.io/cider-documentation/data_formats/cdr.html)
privacyNotes: 1. Data Protection Manual from the IOM (International Organisation for Migration), 2. PPP guidelines from the GSMA (Global System for Mobile Communications Association), 3. Data Protection Handbook for Humanitarian Action from the ICRC (International Committee of the Red Cross). The open source Cider package does not incorporate individual data. Specific deployments of Cider, however, will have to use data sources specific to the project and country. As such, each deployment of Cider will have to be evaluated for its compliance with domestic and international laws. In the case of the Togo deployment, Cider's creators and its implementing partner GiveDirectly worked with the Ministry of Digital Economy and the nation's two telecommunications companies to be compliant with two domestic laws: (1) Data protection (2) Cyber security. In addition to being locally compliant, we have also sought peer review from OCHA's Centre for Humanitarian Data, which has publicly released its evaluation of the tool: https://data.humdata.org/dataset/2048a947-5714-4220-905b-e662cbcd14c8/resource/460e5b29-774a-4bf8-adb4-6c34f11f4987/download/model-report-ucb-cider-model.pdf.
bestPractices: Scalability and Performance/ Scaling and Optimization

We continue to develop and maintain Cider as we use it in collaboration with aid program administrators and the governments of beneficiary countries. Understand the Existing Ecosystem To our knowledge, there are no other tools available built for predicting poverty levels based on mobile phone data. There is a package called Bandicoot which extracts features from CDR (call detail records), a subset of the data we use; Cider gives users the option to delegate to Bandicoot for that step. Design for Scale There is no central bottleneck to more entities using Cider; each runs it locally. A primary goal of registering Cider as a digital public good is to encourage its greater adoption. Be Data Driven Cider exists to make more data-driven decisions around aid targeting. Use Open Standards, Open Data, Open Source, and Open Innovation Cider is open source, and so are all of its dependencies. Reuse and Improve Berkeley and GD have iterated Cider together as we use it, building on our and each other's past work. Cider is also in part built on top of Bandicoot, an existing framework for building models using mobile phone data. Address Privacy & Security Cider is not centralized, so Cider developers do not collect or manage any data. Be Collaborative Cider is open-source and we built it in collaboration with the NGO GiveDirectly. Cider is also used in collaboration with governments and mobile network operators. The hope is that these other organizations could use Cider themselves in the future, without the need for our or GiveDirectly's involvement.

name: CKAN
description: CKAN is an Open Source Data Management System to build Data Portals. Trusted by hundreds of portals across the world and supported by an active community, it focuses on extensibility and integration with other tools.

sdgs.name: SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere
SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.01:
While CKAN is used by many different organizations tackling many different challenges related to the SDGs, it is specially used to help attain SDG 16 (Promote just, peaceful, and inclusive societies). Perhaps the target most contributes to is 16.10 (Ensure public access to information and protect fundamental freedoms) by providing a free, community-led tool for official institutions to publish their data, which is easy to use for users and provides capabilities for advanced users to monitor and explore the datasets. Being widely used by government and civil society institutions to publish open data, it also helps attain among others target 16.6 (Develop effective, accountable, and transparent institutions) by helping publish data about official budgets, expenditures, declared interests etc, allowing citizens to hold institutions accountable.

Other examples where CKAN helps meet the targets of the SDGs include CKAN being used by UNHCR to centralize and standardize refugee-related data, helping with target 10.7 (Facilitating orderly, safe, regular, and responsible migration and mobility of people), and by UNOCHA to host humanitarian data, as well as by several other non-profit organizations working on tackling inequalities around the world (SDG1, SDG10). It is also trusted by many government institutions to publish data that is critical for transparency, accountability and that promotes economic growth (SDG11, SDG8, SDG16). Other organizations like Energinet in Denmark use CKAN to publish energy-related data (SDG7).

nonPIINotes: CKAN is agnostic in terms of the data files and formats that can be published, but strongly promotes the use of generally used standards like CSV or JSON. Data can be published in bulk using the API, and it can be exported in several standard formats including CSV, XML and JSON, both from the user interface and using the API.
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
CKAN uses open standards by design, promoting interoperability via an RPC-style JSON-based API - https://docs.ckan.org/en/2.10/api/index.html, storing reusable configuration in JSON or YAML formats, exporting data as CSV, etc. Via extensions, site maintainers can adopt further standards like DCAT-based metadata, authentication via SAML2 or OAuth2, etc

The CKAN community embraces best practices at all levels, from the development stage using industry-standard open libraries and test-driven development, code reviews, and semantic versioning to the open source community management including community communication channels - https://gitter.im/ckan/chat and the enforcing of a Code of Conduct - https://github.com/ckan/ckan/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity: CKAN follows industry best practices at different levels to safely store sensitive data. At the database level, it encourages secure practices to keep credentials safe, and appropriately encrypts sensitive data like passwords or API tokens. At the application level, datasets can be marked as private so only selected organization users or collaborators have access to them, both in terms of the metadata and to access the actual data. For more complex scenarios, like providing access to just the metadata, certain parts of it, etc maintainers can use the plugins mechanism to customize the authorization further, to make sure it fits their needs. Security audits are regularly performed on existing CKAN sites, and the CKAN maintainers consistently addresses security reports that might lead to the exposure of sensitive data.

name: ClimWeb
description: Open-source platform enabling climate & environmental institutions to deliver services. Features state-of-the-art data visualizations, satellite imagery, user engagement, CAP alerts, digital marketing. Deployed across 30 countries, supporting SDG 13.

sdgRelevance.13: SDG: SDG 13: Climate Action - This is the most directly relevant SDG. ClimWeb directly supports climate action by: Enabling early warning systems for climate-related disasters, facilitating climate data sharing and evidence-based decision-making, supporting climate adaptation and mitigation strategies Improving climate resilience through better information delivery.

openAlternatives: ClimWeb does not rely on any closed-source or proprietary components as mandatory dependencies for its core functionality. References to Google Translate and YouTube relate exclusively to optional, front-end integrations used for content display and user convenience. These services are not required for ClimWeb to operate and can be disabled or replaced without affecting any core system functionality. Translation: The Google Translate widget is an optional client-side integration. ClimWeb fully supports multilingual content management natively, allowing all content to be authored, managed and displayed in multiple languages without reliance on external translation services. Where automatic translation is desired, open-source or self-hosted alternatives (e.g. LibreTranslate, Argos Translate, Marian NMT) can be used instead. Video hosting: YouTube embeds are optional and used only for hosting multimedia content. ClimWeb equally supports self-hosted video files and open-source or federated alternatives (e.g. PeerTube) with no loss of functionality. In all cases, ClimWeb remains fully cloud-agnostic, platform-independent, and deployable on-premises, with no mandatory proprietary dependencies.
nonPIINotes: ClimWeb collects and uses extensive non-PII data and content, including: Meteorological Data: - Weather observations (temperature, precipitation, wind, humidity) - Climate data and historical records - Satellite imagery and remote sensing data - Forecast models and predictions - Aviation weather data (METAR/TAF) Environmental Data: - Air quality measurements - Hydrological data (river levels, rainfall) - Agricultural and environmental monitoring data - Geospatial datasets and maps Content Data: - Weather alerts and warnings (CAP format) - Educational content and resources - News articles and announcements - Data visualizations and charts - User-generated content (comments, feedback) System Data: - Website analytics and usage statistics - Performance metrics and logs - Configuration settings and metadata All of this data is anonymous and cannot be used to identify individuals. The solution is specifically designed for institutional use by meteorological and environmental agencies to manage and disseminate public information services. sdgs.name: SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth

sdgRelevance.04:
Code Your Future is a free training programme for refugees and other people excluded from education and training. Our classes are free, and our teachers are volunteers.

Our free and open-source syllabus is developed and published directly on GitHub. We collaborate with other free code programmes within the MigraCode network (https://migracode.eu/) and ad-hoc in the UK, South Africa, Roma, Medellin, etc.

We do our work in public. We are committed to free, open-source education and curriculum development, and all our materials are published and shared freely. People use our syllabus alone, in a code group, within another coding programme, and within our in-person classes.

Code Your Future is a learning community where total life transformation happens. We understand that transformational change must be challenging but should not be harmful. Our course recognises that change can be difficult. We create spaces of psychological safety, including online spaces, where people can feel supported during a challenging learning journey to starting careers in tech.

Our work largely falls on these targets in SDG 4: - Target 4.3: Equal access to affordable technical, vocational and higher education - Target 4.4: Increase the number of people with relevant skills for financial success - Target 4.5: Eliminate all discrimination in education.

Our work also supports these targets:

5.5 Effective participation and access to the ICT industry and cutting-edge technology. 40% of our trainees are women, while only 12.5% of software engineers in the UK are women.

8.5.1 Hourly earnings & 10.2.1 People living below 50 per cent of median income. 99% of our trainees are on a low income and 83% live in poverty. Graduates from CYF typically move from 1st or 2nd decile income group to the 8th or 9th within six months of graduation.

name: CodeCarbon
description: At CodeCarbon, we believe, as Niels Bohr said, that "Nothing exists until it is measured". So we found a way to estimate how much carbon we produce while running our code. We did this by creating a Python package that estimates your hardware electricity power consumption.

sdgRelevance.12: CodeCarbon allow users to understand how much energy and CO2 emissions are associated with a computer process. Knowing that the user could relocate the process to a region with less carbon-intensive electricity or reduce the electricity consumption with optimisation (Target 12.2, 12.6).

openAlternatives: Core functionality does NOT require proprietary services. The base emissions tracking library works entirely offline with open-source dependencies for CPU and RAM monitoring. Optional proprietary services fall into three categories: 1. Additional features (Fief, Logfire, CO2Signal) - Used only when specific features like API authentication or real-time carbon intensity are needed. 2. Auto-configuration helpers (Geolocation APIs) - Easily bypassed with manual configuration. 3. Hardware-specific (pynvml) - Only required for NVIDIA GPU tracking.

dataPrivacySecurity:
Using temporary access tokens*  for user authentication is a secure practice that limits token validity, thereby reducing the risk of unauthorized access. This approach necessitates periodic reauthentication, ensuring that sessions remain active only for authorized users. Furthermore, storing passwords in a hashed form within the database is crucial for security. Hashing irreversibly transforms passwords into a unique set of characters, safeguarding user credentials even in the event of a data breach. By combining these methods, systems enhance their defense against unauthorized access and potential security threats.

* Storing hashed user emails and expiration dates in JSON Web Tokens (JWT) secures user sessions by encrypting sensitive information and limiting token validity. This approach ensures that tokens expire after a set period, enhancing platform security by necessitating periodic user reauthentication.

name: Community Health Toolkit
description: The CHT is a license-free, open-source digital health platform that includes a collection of software frameworks and applications, open-access resources, and a dynamic community of practice to help partners design, own, and scale electronic community health information systems.

sdgRelevance.03: Medic’s work aligns with SDGs 3, 5, and 17. SDG 3: Our mission is rooted in achieving good health and well-being for all. We strive to advance universal health coverage through our digital solutions and our work actively supports the professionalization of CHWs to deliver these critical services. The CHT goes beyond simple communication; it allows CHWs to track patients and health data, ensuring proper care coordination and follow-up, for example, guiding CHWs to high-risk pregnancies or missed vaccinations. Disease surveillance functions allow CHWs to serve as an early warning system for epidemics. Evidence on the impact of CHT interventions is available here: https://communityhealthtoolkit.org/faqs#faq-09 and via our research archive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/0By87R494_wpBRlJGS052bUVLUzA?resourcekey=0-xEvAOQKY86-qWky9VTvUEg SDG 5: Medic and the CHT community’s advocacy for gender equality is most apparent in our advocacy for better compensation, protective equipment, and support for the mostly female CHWs who are the main users of CHT apps. Examples include a journal article in the BMJ calling for greater involvement of and protection of CHWs in COVID-19 response (https://gh.bmj.com/content/5/6/e002550), and participation in a report (lead author: Resolve to Save Lives) focused on protecting health workers (https://resolvetosavelives.org/about/press/protecting-hcws/). SDG 17: The CHT is recognized as a digital public good, and the public goods approach is all about partnering to achieve the SDGs rather than going alone with a private/proprietary solution. The CHT is included as a digital public good in Digital Square’s Global Goods Guidebook (https://digitalsquare.org/resourcesrepository/2023/5/25/global-goods-guidebook-version-40) and is featured as a global good in a USAID, WHO, and ITU supported course in Digital Health: Planning National Systems (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gxf0xNvZPG8).

Principles for Digital Development, Responsive design, Offline-first progressive web apps
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
It is important to note that the CHT does not itself directly collect PII. Rather, the CHT community builds a framework and other foundational technologies that make it easier for health systems to implement their own CHT apps. CHT apps are highly configurable and it is up to the relevant Data Controlling Entity for each CHT app to determine what PII will be collected. Common examples include name, age, phone number, geolocation, personal health information including care encounters and test results, highly sensitive health information including HIV status, and data relevant to the social determinants of health such as level of education and wealth quintile.

Privacy policy differs per app and it is the responsibility of the Data Controlling Entity (such as a Ministries of Health) to establish such policies. The CHT community grants Data Controlling Entities the freedom to establish their policies, which is essential to the terms of our OSI-approved open-source license. The following are the steps taken to prevent adverse impact related to PII: Encryption, isolation, and restrictive permissions.
contentManagement: Content is NOT collected NOT stored and NOT distributed.
harrassmentPolicy: Most CHT apps are designed specifically for use by health workers and user accounts are provided by organizations such that access is not available to the general public. In CHT apps that support messaging with patients, the relevant patients are enrolled and consented by a trained health worker. To our knowledge, there have not been any deployments of CHT apps in which minors were enrolled to use the system. One of the four core principles of the CHT community is that we are committed to designing CHT systems in a human-centered manner. In our view, this is not merely a buzzword or a statement of ethical priorities. Rather, it is a set of rigorous methods that work within a flexible yet disciplined process to prioritize people’s needs and concrete experiences in the design of digital systems. An essential feature of human-centered design is that it prioritizes the dignity and agency of end users. It is also explicitly iterative and takes responsibility for making adaptations to address any potential unintended effects of a system – such as a situation in which health workers might experience grief or abuse from a peer or supervisor via their digital tool. We have conducted extensive research and members of our team are considered global authorities on the topic of human-centered design for global health, and we consider this approach to be a thorough and substantive means of addressing lived experiences of harassment and abuse in health systems. More about CHT principles and our human-centered design approach in the following links: https://communityhealthtoolkit.org/principles https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02681102.2019.1667289

name: Connect For Life
description: Connect for Life is a communication platform built on OpenMRS. The platform engages with patients remotely and provides continuity of care with proven implementation feasibility in HIV, TB, and COVID-19 case surveillance and vaccination programs.

sdgRelevance.03:
Educational health content customized per disease can be shared through the Connect For Life platform with the targeted patient population and this can impact the following SDG targets:
SDG 3.3.1: Using the communication from Connect For Life, patients can be stimulated to adhere to their HIV medication intakes and in so doing reduce their risk of transmission to other non-infected individuals. Educational content can also be shared in a discrete fashion to ensure that risks of transmission are known. This educational content can be important for many HIV patient groups such as adolescents, MSM, HIV-infected pregnant women to help prevent transmission to sexual contacts and or to unborn babies.
SDG 3.3.2: For TB patients adherence to medication for longer treatment periods is critical to achieve cure. Messages from Connect For Life can take the form of engaging, actionable instructions to help motivate individuals to adhere to therapy and thereby help them to reach care and preventing further transmission.

privacyNotes: Connect For Life has been developed under consideration of privacy relevant standards, including security and privacy by design (see more details on the webpage: https://github.com/johnsonandjohnson/openmrs-distro-cfl/wiki/Software-Terms-Of-Use) Connect for Life platform was part of an external review of our digital assets in light of GDPR and African Union (AU) equivalent regulations: GDPR AU Treaty

dataPrivacySecurity:
Data in the system is being encrypted in transit (HTTPS TLS 1.3) as well as in rest, depending on the configuration (e.g. AES-256). Passwords are additionally encrypted following the OpenMRS standard via SHA-512. Access to the system is user based controlled with different roles and responsibilities that segregate administrators from the regular users.

contentManagement: Content is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
contentManagementPolicy: Any content shared with patients through Connect for Life™ is required in clinical study context to be approved by the relevant ethical committee(s) or health authorities. There is no advertising push from the system to patients nor is any non-approved content distributed via this channel. Connect for Life™ does not provide provide doctor’s advice. The system provides generic health information and nothing is customized at the individual patient level. Surveys can be delivered that allow for the patient to provide information. These questionnaires are also subjected to approval by the relevant ethical committee(s) or health authorities and are offered as multiple-choice answers without the option of adding free text. Other types of content collected and stored are: language preference of the user, adherence to visit schedule (in context of attendance at clinic for a study protocol schedule), whether end user has picked up their phone or not. standardsAndPracticesNotes: [1] User Stories: Clearly define and prioritize user stories based on business value. Use a collaborative approach involving stakeholders to gather and refine user stories. Keep user stories small, specific, and independent for efficient development. [2] Change Management Using Version Control: Utilize version control systems (e.g., Git) to track changes in the codebase. Follow a branching strategy (e.g., Git Flow) to manage feature development, bug fixes, and releases. Implement commit message standards for clear communication and traceability. [3] Test-Driven Development (TDD) Using Automated Tests: Use unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests to ensure comprehensive test coverage. Incorporate continuous testing into the development process. [4] Continuous Integration & Continuous Deployment (CI/CD): Integrate code changes frequently to a shared repository. Automate the build and deployment processes. Implement continuous testing, and if tests pass, automate the deployment pipeline. [5] Model–View–Controller (MVC): Separate the application logic into Model, View, and Controller components. Enhance maintainability and scalability by following the MVC architectural pattern. [6] Representational State Transfer (REST): Design RESTful APIs with resource-oriented URLs. Use HTTP methods appropriately (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) for CRUD operations. Implement stateless communication and utilize standard HTTP status codes. [7] Cloud Computing (AWS): Leverage scalable and resilient cloud services. Implement security best practices, including identity and access management (IAM). Optimize resources for cost efficiency and performance. [8] Open Source: Follow open-source licensing standards and document licenses. Encourage community collaboration through transparent communication channels (Slack) Regularly update documentation and engage with the user community.

name: cQube
description: cQube is an open-source platform for data-based insights. It allows for aggregated data to be visualized in a simple fashion, leading to insights and action. It provides flexibility and ease of use in creating dashboards, enabling business user to derive insights.

sdgRelevance.04:
Saral can be used across domains for applications that require quick and seamless phygitization of data - capture of physical data in a digital, structured format. This results in significant savings in terms of time and effort that would otherwise be required in order to capture the physical data in a digital format.

Sunbird Saral has been successfully used by the state government of the largest state in India (Uttar Pradesh) to conduct state-wide assessments tests for about 17 million students from grade 1 to grade 8 - in order to garner a grassroots level understanding of the learning gaps, as well as the needs and challenges faced by the students.

The state had a strong desire to gain a deeper understanding of student performance in order to effectively cater to various programs and student learning needs, which aim to achieve universal foundational literacy and numeracy in primary schools by 2025.  However, traditional assessment methods bring forth several challenges - these methods were not at scale or student level, making it difficult to obtain reliable data for the state to make informed decisions. Additionally, the time it took for data to reach the central department from traditional assessment methods was too long, as the process involved physical question paper preparation, exam conduction, answer sheet evaluation, result generation and then manually digitizing results, leading to a delay of up to three to four months.

The Saral solution replaces the old answer sheets with OMR-based answer sheets and allows teachers to scan the answer sheet through the Saral App. This process instantly digitizes data and allows the state to receive digitized data on the very same day of scanning. Quick and detailed information provided by Saral Assessments has empowered decision-makers to make data-driven choices and take prompt action to enhance educational outcomes in the state.

The state is now also planning for a pilot program to explore the use of Saral for other teacher-led activities such as new student admissions to schools. The app can be used to quickly scan admission forms of students and transfer the data to the state backend systems, resulting in significant saving of time for the teachers.

Thus, there is no long-term storage of individual user data (temporarily processed and purged) to prevent the possibility of such data being exposed to unauthorized persons. cQube  software has implemented data collection in an open and transparent manner. cQube software implements principles of minimalism,  transparency of data collection, and other best practices. Implementers/adopters of cQube, have the autonomy to decide “what” fields to  capture/maintain, “what” other systems will they integrate with, “will” they share this data with other authorized parties (e.g. one Government sharing this dataset with other Government, or one Department sharing this dataset with other Department). name: Crosscut
description: The Crosscut App lets users access open data including catchment area maps, microplan tables that estimate population, and supply plan tables that can be used to plan Global Health campaigns.

sdgRelevance.03: Health program managers often miss coverage, equity, and cost goals because they cannot easily and affordably access quality information below the district level. Achieving these goals often involves costly, recurring technical assistance. The Crosscut app is a technology that helps to solve this problem by allowing non-technical health program staff to independently create catchment area maps, estimate target populations, analyze geographic accessibility, and make effective plans at the sub-district level. This “microplanning” helps to ensure settlements are not missed, services are provided equitably, and the right quantity of supplies is where they need to be. We aim to "de-expert" microplanning, and our vision is for any user to be able to quickly do geospatial microplanning without the need for outside experts.

name: Decidim
description: Decidim is a digital platform for citizen participation

sdgRelevance.10: SDG10: Citizen participation mechanisms are traditionally held in person. Providing a digital channel for participation enables people who are home-bound, people who are busy at work when participatory events happen, or people who are otherwise unable to attend, to take part in participatory processes as well. SDG16: In order for participatory democracy processes to be legitimate, they need to be transparent and audited. Decidim provides transparency to each decision taken within a participatory process by making every vote, discussion, proposal and participation, open and published, so that a digital archive of the process remains for any needed audits. Decidim has also worked to implement traceability mechanisms against tampering which are reflected in Decidim's social contract: https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/understand/social-contract#_transparency_traceability_and_integrity

ownershipEvidence: The creation of the association was decided in a community assembly recorded on our own governance Decidim instance: https://meta.decidim.org/assemblies/our-governance The decision was formalized in the statues of the association that can be consulted here: https://metadecidim.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/decidim/attachment/file/2096/ESTATUTS_ASS_DECIDIM__AMB_ESMENESV2_.pdf
nonPIINotes: It’s possible to export data in multiple formats: CSV, JSON, and XLSX. Decidim also comes with an API based on GraphQL.
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
Using open standards is in our social contract: https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/understand/social-contract.html#_free_software_and_open_content - WCAG 2.0/2.1 (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) -> https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/develop/guide_accessibility.html - SSL / HTTPS: https://docs.decidim.org/en/v0.27/configure/initializer.html#_force_ssl - AES-256: For several of its processes Decidim uses AES-256 encryption. Examples are Voting module https://docs.decidim.org/bulletin-board/admin/virtual-voting-booth.html#_ballot_encryption or encrypting personal identifieble information. It does so by using Ruby on Rail's ActiveSupport::MesageEncryptor https://api.rubyonrails.org/v5.2.3/classes/ActiveSupport/MessageEncryptor.html https://github.com/decidim/decidim/blob/v0.27.3/decidim-core/lib/decidim/attribute_encryptor.rb - OAuth/OpenID: Decidim is integrated with OAuth, both as a provider in itself, as a client. You can check more here https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/customize/oauth.html - JWT are part of our architecture https://github.com/decidim/decidim/blob/v0.27.3/Gemfile.lock#L355 - UTF-8 Decidim takes UTF-8 as its official, internal encoding. https://github.com/decidim/decidim/blob/2037eeb12a9cec666e74fe9b3dfb7c22c2f2597e/decidim-core/lib/decidim/io_encoder.rb#L9 - Decidim's front-end is written in HTML, CSS and Javascript complying code - GraphQL: Decidim comes with a powerful API in read-only mode based in the GraphQL specification. https://docs.decidim.org/en/v0.27/develop/api.html - JSON: Decidim uses JSON extensibly in its code https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Adecidim%2Fdecidim+JSON&type=code

- Translations: Decidim has been translated by the open source community into 55 languages (https://github.com/decidim/decidim/tree/develop/decidim-core/config/locales) for this we use Crowdin, a service that allows anyone who has even a few minutes to spare, to volunteer translating snippets into their language. More information about our translation process here: https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/contribute/translations.html - Governance: The software and the project Decidim is steered by its community. We do so in a democratic way by participating in a Decidim instance which help us make decisions. The instance is MetaDecidim and can be checked here: meta.decidim.org/ We also hold a list of principles which guide us into any decisions we take. These are here https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/understand/social-contract you can understand more about our governance here https://meta.decidim.org/processes/Welcome - Testing: Every time a Pull request is opened, our Continuous Integration tools run several tests, among them is to check for test coverage. This means the code will not passed unless enough tests are written and passed. We use SimpleCov and CodeCov to check for test coverage. We have guides for testers here https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/develop/testing and you can check results of our tests here: https://app.codecov.io/github/decidim/decidim - CI/CD: Decidim receives a lot of contributions. According to Repotracker.com, we receive in average 3.2 Pull requests per day (source: https://repo-tracker.com/r/gh/decidim/decidim). As such, integration and deployment tools are very important to us. They do everything from check test coverage, integrate translations, check code linting, building docker images, etc. All of our CI/CD tools are open and available at https://github.com/decidim/decidim/tree/develop/.github/workflows - Contributions (code reviews, agile, etc): Decidim has an active pool of contributors located worldwide that are sending a number of contributions each day. As such, code reviewing and feedback, as well as general discussion about technology decisions is very important. As with everything, all of these activities happen in the open. For this, we use the comment section on PRs (which incidentally also remains as a valuable resource for learning developers), here is such an example: https://github.com/decidim/decidim/pull/10954 we also make extensive use of Github's discussion forums to make technical decisions open https://github.com/decidim/decidim/discussions and finally, we have an element channel open to everyone for shorter term questions at chat.decidim.org our organization mode uses agile to deliver in short spans of time. You can view our open project boards here: https://github.com/decidim/decidim/projects?type=classic additionally, we ensure we provide contributors with enough resources to start developing. Among others, we use Gitflow to name our branches https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/develop/guide_conventions and provide extensive developer guides https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/develop/ - 12 factor apps: Decidim follows 12 factor recommendations https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/develop/guide#_good_to_know - Architectural design: Decidim was built as a ruby gem (a library). This was a very conscious decision that was made to enable any decidim instances in the wild to upgrade with little pain, no matter how old. We recommend you read this short post where we explain our decisions about the architecture we chose: https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/develop/guide_example_apps.html as for other descriptors, Decidim uses the RoR Engines pattern, it is component based, which enables any admin to design their own processes, as a Rails app, it runs under the MVC paradigm. - UX/UI: Decidim has stayed with its UI design for the totality of its life. Although its interface can be easily overwritten, a redesign is much needed. As with everything the process has been open and collaborative. We have a participatory process on meta decidim where open calls happen, discussions are held and decisions taken. You can view some of it here: https://meta.decidim.org/processes/RedesignDecidim/f/1663/?locale=en the redesign process is also tracked using a scrum board here: https://github.com/decidim/decidim/projects/23 - Standard for Public Code: We have followed the project of the Standard for Public Code since its inception, inviting them to our 2019 Decidim Fest edition and acting as invitees for their Let's talk about public code podcast https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MFAb8QaDXFY&ab_channel=FoundationforPublicCode

dataPrivacySecurity:
Decidim instances (not decidim itself!) collect the data necessary to ensure people can participate. A base decidim installation will require a username, name, email and password. Decidim offers an authorizations module, which allows organizations to require more data to verify the users should they want to make a process that has eligibility rules for participation. A use case for this would be collecting the user's neighborhood for a process that's constricted to neighbors only. Here's more information about the Authorizations module https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/customize/authorizations

Decidim is designed so that only the minimum information to operate about the users is public. For actions that involve public discussion such as comments and proposals, a username, name and profile picture is included. User profiles only show these 3 data points (example: https://meta.decidim.org/profiles/txema/activity). Emails cannot be viewed by either other users or admins. Should an admin or user want to get in touch with another user, they would need to use the messaging feature. Any non-public fields, such as passwords and tokens are encrypted by default. In compliance with GDPR, Decidim offers a feature to download all your data and delete your account. Administrators are required to add a Terms and Conditions declaration that is presented to users at sign-up. Changes to the Terms and conditions page are reported back to end users so that they have the option of re-accepting them. In accordance with our social contract, data integrity is very important to the legitimacy of participatory processes. Decidim is coded with a heavy reliance on action logging which ensure all changes done to participatory processes are traceable. For this we use the Papertrail library: https://github.com/paper-trail-gem/paper_trail the application also operates all actions under a permission system. You can find more information here: https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/develop/permissions.html Experimental features in democratic data integrity: In the case of Elections, we are working on a module that encrypts votes in every step of the way. We also partnered with Vocdoni to build a blockchain-based voting module. name: DHIS2
description: DHIS2 is a free, open-source, fully customizable platform for collecting, analyzing, visualizing, and sharing aggregate and individual-data for district-level, national, regional, and international system and program management in health, education, and other domains.

sdgRelevance.03:
DHIS2 is the world's largest Health Management Information System platform, and is currently in use in more than 80 low- and middle-income countries, 74 are deployed at national scale. DHIS2 is also used by national health authorities and international health organizations (such as WHO, the CDC, PEPFAR, The Global Fund, Gavi) for management of specific health programs, such as HIV, TB, Malaria, immunization, and disease surveillance. The large-scale adoption of DHIS2 has enabled countries to leverage it to rapidly respond to emerging crises such as the Covid-19 pandemic.

New DHIS2 tools for Climate & Health facilitate incorporation of climate, weather, and environmental data into DHIS2 to support analysis, modeling, and forecasting of climate-sensitive health risks and help improve the climate resilience of national health systems. DHIS2 has also developed a module for last-mile logistics intended for use at the health facility level and integrated with a central eLMIS or ERP. The features include report and transaction-based stock management, equipment management, and temperature monitoring. In addition to health, DHIS2 is also now being deployed as an Education Management Information System (EMIS) in several countries, which facilitates more effective triangulation of data between health and education programs (for example, vaccination campaigns targeting school-aged children), as well as supporting purely education-related goals.

openAlternatives: The platform can be optionally configured to use Google Analytics, Google Maps, Bing Maps, and Google Earth Engine for additional capabilities, but they are not mandatory dependencies.
nonPIINotes: Non-PII data can be extracted and/or imported using the DHIS2 Web API as described here: https://docs.dhis2.org/en/develop/using-the-api/dhis-core-version-239/introduction.html and via the Import-Export App within DHIS2. Data can be exported/imported in common formats including CSV, XML and JSON, as well as the standard ADX format (https://docs.dhis2.org/archive/en/2.29/developer/html/webapi_adx_data_format.html) for aggregate data exchange.
privacyNotes: Compliance with data and legal frameworks in the context of DHIS2 is entirely an implementation issue. The HISP Centre at UiO is responsible for developing the DHIS2 software, but does not collect or host any country’s health data. We do provide guidance on how to implement DHIS2 in compliance with various standards, and are aware of DHIS2 implementations that have been certified as HIPAA and ISO 27000 compliant, for example. As an example of GDPR compliance, the Norwegian municipal government association reviewed their DHIS2 implementation for COVID-19 surveillance and found it to be GDPR compliant. https://docs.dhis2.org/en/implement/implementing-dhis2/security-considerations.html?h=gdpr#legal-and-regulatory-context
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
DHIS2 software is provided with tools and guidelines to mitigate security and privacy risks. Proper adherence to these is the responsibility of each individual organization that implements the DHIS2 software, since each instance of the software is locally owned and maintained, and the DHIS2 core team does not have access to individual country databases. To the extent that the University of Oslo is involved in implementation of the software in-country -- either directly or via our HISP network -- we strive to adhere to best practices for data security and privacy, in accordance with local laws. DHIS2 features configurable access control levels that restrict access to specific kinds of information to particular user roles, groups, and organization units. Additionally, metadata can be defined as either public or private. The DHIS2 database itself can be encrypted.

A discussion of some privacy controls can be found here: https://community.dhis2.org/t/how-does-dhis2-protect-personal-information-the-tech-details/5335/2 https://docs.dhis2.org/en/implement/android-implementation/data-security-and-privacy.html

An overview of DHIS2's built-in security and privacy features can be found here: https://dhis2.org/security/

harrassmentPolicy:
Interactions between users / contributors on this project are managed through an online forum, the DHIS2 Community of Practice: https://community.dhis2.org. You can find out code of conduct and moderation information here: https://community.dhis2.org/about.

The target audience for this community is skilled users of the DHIS2 software (expected age 20+), and discussion is limited to topics relating to software implementation and use. The age limit for participation on the forum is set at 13 or older. At this point, we have no reason to believe that any underage users are participating in our forum. In regards to the DHIS2 software itself, access controls are established by the countries or organizations implementing the software, which is targeted at professional users. The DHIS2 discussion forum is governed by clearly stated community guidelines: https://community.dhis2.org/faq and is actively moderated by members of the DHIS2 core team, who can flag and remove content or comments as needed.
