name: DiCRA
description: Data in Climate Resilient Agriculture (DiCRA) is a collaborative geospatial platform which provides open access to key geospatial datasets pertinent to climate resilient agriculture. These datasets are curated and validated through collaborative efforts of a large community of data scientists and citizen scientists across the world. The pattern detection and data insights emerging from DiCRA are aimed towards strengthening evidence-driven policy making for climate resilient food systems.

sdgRelevance.13:
The objective of the DiCRA platform is to provide free and open access to geospatial datasets through an open digital platform thereby enabling concrete evidence-driven policies and concerted action from all stakeholders involved in sustainable and climate-resilient agriculture. Through geospatial analysis and data-powered positive deviance approaches, the platform informs stakeholders on which farms are more resilient to extreme weather events. Indigenous knowledge is tapped through field validation and ethnography to suggest good practices on climate-resilient farming that are already working well through bottom-up approaches, to feed into large-scale agriculture programs and policies and optimize public investments in climate-resilient agriculture.  DiCRA platform, therefore, contributes to SDG 2 to 'End hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture'. Specifically, DiCRA contributes to SDG target 2.4 which states 'By 2030, ensure sustainable food production systems and implement resilient agricultural practices that increase productivity and production, that help maintain ecosystems, that strengthen capacity for adaptation to climate change, extreme weather, drought, flooding, and other disasters and that progressively improve land and soil quality. ,

DiCRA platform contributes to SDG 13 'Take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts'. With its objective to enhance climate adaptation measures through data-driven approaches as well as the impact on policies for climate resilient agriculture, the DiCRA platform contributes directly to SDG target 13.1 'Strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity to climate-related hazards and natural disasters in all countries' and SDG target 13.2 to 'Integrate climate change measures into national policies, strategies and planning'.

openAlternatives:
1. DiCRA platform requires the functionality to allow policy-makers to search for a village or locality to perform analysis on climate and agriculture indicators. This requires an API that allows for geocoding (the process of converting address in text format to geo-coordinates). We explored the use of (open option) OSM Geocoder - Nominatim for this but found that the spatial accuracy and match rate is low for our preliminary area of interest which was Telangana. Hence we have used Google Geocoding API for this use case. In case the developer wishes to deploy the application without using this API, the codebase includes the following module which uses Nominatim instead of Google API.
 2. Based on our visual identity and user experience discussions, we have used the CARTO base map public styles (not the proprietary style)as the base map for our map views. It provides a BSD 3-Clause License for the code and CC-BY 4.0 for the design. But it does have the following limitations:
 -- free usage for up to 75,000 map views per month
-- none-commercial services only.
This service does not need to enable an API or an account to set up the base map. If the dark theme is not required, the developer can use alternatives quite easily by updating the code base use services such as Open Map Tiles.
 3. DiCRA also includes a Satellite View which uses the Google Basemap which requires an account registration as well as setting up of API. But the codebase also includes an option to reconfigure it to use USGS or ESRI Base maps instead of Google service.

Effective local government, which is able to provide local infrastructure and services, is key to inclusive development at the last mile, and enabling local governments to collect resources and deliver services in an efficient & transparent manner enhances their capacity to deliver the conditions for well-being, sustainability, and innovation. Our work also aligns with Target 9.c, leveraging local intermediaries to provide digitally-enabled access to services to populations that may otherwise have to rely on physical channels, or have difficulty accessing services at all., At eGov, we see our work as fitting with the themes of SDG 11 - Sustainable Cities and Communities - and SDG 17 - Partnerships for Development. name: DKAN
description: DKAN is a powerful, community-driven open data platform. As a Drupal module, DKAN leverages Drupal's robust features to create modern, standards-focused, and API-first open data catalogs for a variety of specific use cases.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.09: DKAN is utilized by a wide range of organizations, and as an open-source platform, its full impact in supporting the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is wide-ranging. One of its primary contributions is toward SDG 9 (Industry¸ Innovation and Infrastructure). As an open data repository, DKAN also plays a key role in advancing SDG 16.10 (Ensure public access to information and protect fundamental freedoms) by offering a free, community-driven tool for official institutions to easily publish their data. The platform is user-friendly, making data accessible to the public, while also providing advanced capabilities for users who need to monitor and explore datasets in greater detail. Additionally, DKAN contributes to SDG 16.6 (Develop effective, accountable, and transparent institutions) by enabling the publication of open data related to government budgets, expenditures, and declared interests. This transparency helps citizens hold institutions accountable. Widely adopted by governments and civil society organizations, DKAN supports not only transparency and accountability but also economic growth and sustainable development, aligning with SDGs 8, 11, and 16. Trusted by many government institutions, DKAN is a critical tool for fostering transparency and driving progress toward these global goals.

nonPIINotes: DKAN is an open source software platform, based on the Drupal CMS, designed to empower site owners. Because DKAN can be used, hosted, modified, and extended in any environment, full compliance cannot be guaranteed. Compliance ultimately depends on the implementation choices of the site owner and the specifics of their hosting environment. The software’s design alone is not sufficient without the adopted best practices of the site owner utilizing a DKAN-based solution. DKAN is agnostic regarding the types of data files and formats that can be published, while strongly promoting the use of widely adopted standards like CSV and JSON. Data can be published in bulk using the API, and exported in various standard formats, including CSV, XML, and JSON, through both the user interface and the API. There are DKAN sites actively used in compliance with various digital privacy regulations and laws currently in force, including but not limited to: EU: GDPR; and the US.
privacyNotes: DKAN complies with the same privacy, domestic and other applicable international laws as Drupal. As such, DKAN can be implemented in compliance with every digital privacy regulation and law currently under enforcement, including but not limited to: EU: GDPR; US: CCPA, ADA, Section 508, FEDRAMP, HIPAA; Aus: Privacy Act + Privacy Amendment; Brazil: LGPD; Canada: CDA; DCIA, Chile: Ley 19,628; India: PDPB; etc.
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
DKAN uses open standards by design, promoting interoperability through an RPC-style JSON-based API and supporting formats like JSON, YAML, and CSV. This allows for us to store reusable configurations and easily export data. Site maintainers can leverage standards such as Open API, JSON-based API, REST, and authentication via SAML2 or OAuth2. DKAN also ships with the DCAT-US metadata schema, which is a variation of DCAT-based metadata (https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat-3). Because it is all built in Drupal other modules can be added to extend the default functionality. 

Because we leverage Drupal, we work along with Drupal’s best practices. Our project benefits from the code and principles of the Drupal community. With DKAN, automated tests are run on every pull request, as is evident in our main repository (https://github.com/GetDKAN/dkan). This currently includes 92% of DKAN’s code. We also run code climate on each run for code quality (https://codeclimate.com/github/GetDKAN/dkan).
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
DKAN places no restriction on the content that can be hosted by it, so it is up to site maintainers to ensure that it is appropriate and legal for data to be published.

How DKAN handles sensitive personal information (PII) mostly depends on how each site owner implements it. DKAN itself uses secure coding practices and automated testing, but the main job of protecting personal data falls to the site owners. DKAN gives guidelines on secure development, and its security team offers resources to help developers write more secure code. Some companies that provide DKAN-based services have implemented ways to manage personal data that follow rules like HIPAA and other security standards. DKAN also takes advantage of all the security best practices built into Drupal.
contentManagement: Content is collected stored and distributed.
contentManagementPolicy: DKAN has the same policies in place as Drupal, as it is a Drupal module. As per Drupal: Ultimately, site owners are individually responsible for the content policies they enact when using Drupal to build a content platform in their jurisdiction. Drupal provides a variety of tools and integrations that can be used to help prevent the submission of inappropriate or illegal content. When content is being entered by a centrally managed editorial team, site owners can implement tools provided by: https://www.drupal.org/docs/8/core/modules/content-moderation/overview When content is user-generated or user-submitted, Drupal site owners can implement integration with third party tools such as the Google Cloud Vision API to aid in inappropriate/illegal content detection, and/or implement community moderation tools such as content flagging/reporting. Use of inappropriate/illegal content is also against the Drupal's community code of conduct and values and principles: https://www.drupal.org/dcoc https://www.drupal.org/about/values-and-principles Finally, Drupal.org itself, the community website where open source contributors come together to build Drupal, has a firm stance against inappropriate and illegal content and both staff and community moderators help protect the community's home. https://www.drupal.org/terms

sdgRelevance.08:
Drupal supports Sustainable Development Goals in 2 parallel ways:

Direct support, in which the Drupal project itself advances the goals.
Indirect support, in which Drupal empowers other organizations to advance the SDGs.

In fact, https://sdgs.un.org/goals is a Drupal site! In addition, there are other already recognized Digital Public Goods, such as FarmOS (https://www.drupal.org/project/farm), that are built with Drupal as the foundation.

===========
Direct support:
===========

===========
8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
===========

Target 8.2: Diversify, innovate, and upgrade for economic productivity
Target 8.5: Full employment and decent work with equal pay

Because Drupal is an innovative and market-leading software platform--that is open source and based on common technology standards--provides direct opportunities for economic empowerment.

As an open-source project with robust multilingual support and a global community of contributors, Drupal is available to anyone, without licensing fees, dramatically lowering the start-up cost of digital business for entrepreneurs around the world.

Furthermore, Drupal jobs are tech jobs, not gate-kept traditional degrees or mandatory certifications, and can be done from anywhere in the world.

As an open-source project, Drupal supports entrepreneurs who want to build a new business opportunity on the web. This is reflected in the nearly 1 million websites using Drupal today: https://www.drupal.org/project/usage/drupal

On the enterprise scale as well, analysts like Gartner and Forrester see significant economic opportunities in the use of open-source software: https://www.forrester.com/blogs/what-open-sources-collision-with-paas-means-for-drupal-and-wordpress-services-forr-in-3-video/

There is also an ecosystem of more than a thousand Drupal agencies hiring Drupal talent in nearly every country in the world, and tens of thousands of end-users who need the same talent. Because Drupal is a widely adopted technology in both the private and public sectors, Drupal empowers those who learn it with more bargaining power and more opportunities for jobs in Open Source technology. Demand is high enough that the Drupal Association maintains jobs.drupal.org as a platform to connect talented Drupal developers to employment opportunities.
https://www.drupal.org/drupal-services
https://jobs.drupal.org
https://www.indeed.com/jobs?q=Drupal+Developer&l=&vjk=c4545e0824ca3195

Finally, communities all over the world have local associations that connect emerging Drupal talent with economic opportunities in their area:
https://www.drupal.org/node/3069614

===========
10: Reduced Inequalities
===========

Target 10.1: Reduce income inequalities
Target 10.2: Promote universal social, economic, and political inclusion

Open source software such as Drupal offers a counter-balance to traditional economic models that extract resources from developing nations rather than providing them with resources. An internet based on proprietary technology, patents, and trademarks replicates the wealth extraction of private industry and crowds out entrepreneurship. It puts wealth and value in only a few hands.

In contrast Drupal and the open web focus on providing a free and open internet, where that economic opportunity is accessible to all. In particular, Drupal empowers low-income users around the globe in two key ways.

Entrepreneurship - In the last two decades, entrepreneurs have built businesses based on Drupal all over the world, participating in an ecosystem of almost $4 billion of economic activity. Many of these entrepreneurs are from economically disadvantaged and underprivileged regions of the world.

privacyNotes:
Because Drupal is a software platform that can be used, hosted, modified, extended, etc by any user in any environment, it is designed to empower site owners to adhere to international laws and regulations as easily as possible. However, compliance cannot be guaranteed, because in all cases full compliance depends on the implementation choices of the site owner, and the details of their hosting environment. The design of the software alone is not sufficient without the adopted best practices of the site owner or SaaS vendor with a solution built on top of Drupal. That said there are Drupal sites actively used in compliance with every digital privacy regulation and law currently under enforcement, including but not limited to: EU: GDPR; US: CCPA, ADA, Section 508, FEDRAMP, HIPAA; Aus: Privacy Act + Privacy Amendment; Brazil: LGPD; Canada: CDA; DCIA, Chile: Ley 19,628; India: PDPB; etc, etc.


Drupal's compliance, like any software platform in isolation, is based on the specific end-user building on top of it. However, Drupal endeavors to make it as easy as possible to comply with domestic and international regulations. Some resources Drupal provides: https://www.drupal.org/docs/getting-started/accessibility/accessibility-conformance-report-acr-process https://www.drupal.org/docs/extending-drupal/contributed-modules/contributed-modules/general-data-protection-regulation/getting-started https://www.drupal.org/project/drupal_gdpr_team Contributed modules that aid site owners in compliance: https://www.drupal.org/project/gdpr https://www.drupal.org/project/gdpr_compliance 3rd party (not managed or directed by the Drupal Association) Saas providers who have built offerings on top of Drupal that offer compliance support: https://docs.acquia.com/cloud-platform/arch/security/compliance-standards-and-regulations/ https://pantheon.io/security https://platform.sh/security/ https://www.amazee.io/industry/government Many government institutions are using Drupal for their own web portals, demonstrating their own compliance with their regulations using Drupal as the platform: The European Commission itself has built their web presence on Drupal, and notes their use of Drupal in their compliance statement: https://commission.europa.eu/cookies-policy_en The United Nations web presence is also built on Drupal, as the platform for their digital compliance: https://un.org GovCMS which is used for Australia's entire digital web presence in compliance with local and international regulations is built on Drupal: https://www.govcms.gov.au/ and many others.

When content is user-generated or user-submitted, Drupal site owners can implement integration with third party tools such as the Google Cloud Vision API to aid in inappropriate/illegal content detection, and/or implement community moderation tools such as content flagging/reporting.


Use of inappropriate/illegal content is also against the Drupal's community code of conduct and values and principles:
https://www.drupal.org/dcoc
https://www.drupal.org/about/values-and-principles

Finally, Drupal.org itself, the community website where open source contributors come together to build Drupal, has a firm stance against inappropriate and illegal content and both staff and community moderators help protect the community's home.

https://www.drupal.org/terms

name: E-Heza
description: E-Heza Data Solutions is a digital health platform designed by and for frontline health workers that serves the entire primary care ecosystem of health centers and CHWs in East Africa.

sdgs.name: SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth

sdgRelevance.02:
E-Heza is used to support community-based nutrition programs and to screen patients for signs of malnutrition in order to suggest early intervention and referral to nutrition programs as necessary. Data collected in E-Heza supports reporting on all SDG 2.2 indicators. Additionally, E-Heza will be used to monitor the impact of Rwanda’s national nutrition and childhood development program.  In the health centers that have implemented E-Heza, there has been a 27% drop in severe malnutrition after three visits. ,

E-Heza supports the good health and well being goal by providing healthcare workers with an efficient interface for providing maternal and child healthcare according to protocols and international standards, and to pass patient data, including diagnosis and treatments, across levels of care.    Among the hundreds of healthcare workers using E-Heza, quality of care has been shown to have increased by 120% and have documented 150 minutes saved per patient interaction. E-Heza supports comprehensive primary care across the entire spectrum of maternal and child health, as well as non-communicable diseases of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Data collected can easily provide reports on most SDG indicators, particularly for SDG 3.1 (Decrease global maternal mortality), SDG 3.2 (End preventable deaths of newborns and children under 5), SDG 3.3 (Fight communicable diseases), SDG 3.4 (Reduce mortality from non-communicable diseases and promote mental health), and SDG 3.8 (Achieve Universal Health Coverage- RMNCH branch).

The vast majority of frontline health workers (70%) in East Africa are women; yet, less than 25% of women  hold  leadership roles that give them authority to improve the systems where they work. Female frontline health workers are generally paid 28%  less than men for comparable work in East Africa, and are more likely to suffer from burnout. Burnout is known to contribute to poor quality care. These conditions are even worse in the rural (Rwanda and Burundi)  and peri-urban (Somalia)  areas where we work. By decreasing workloads and nurturing the passion of frontline health workers, care quality is improving, families are participating in their care, and health outcomes are improving. This allows us to impact SDG5 (Gender Equity) and SDG8 (Decent Work) by decreasing workloads and strengthening skills of frontline health workers.

dataPrivacySecurity:
E-Heza adheres to all 'Do No Harm' policies established by our parent organization, TIP Global Health. This policy is available here - https://tip-global-health.github.io/eheza-documentation/policy_docs/do-no-harm/.  E-Heza's 'Do No Harm' approach focuses on patient and caregiver safety by:
1. Preventing Errors:
 -
E-Heza's decision logic model and all aspects of clinical care are governed by a clinical review process that includes physicians, healthcare workers, and digital health specialists. This work is reviewed by the E-Heza Executive committee.
- Development work is open source and follows a peer review process in which all code is first reviewed by another developer before it is submitted to the QA process.
- E-Heza adheres to best practices  privacy and data security standards to ensure the protection of private patient information.
2. Learning from mistakes:
- TIP Global Health's Model is based on gathering feedback and acting on it. There is a regular process of understanding challenges and potential errors which may cause harm. (https://tipglobalhealth.org/our-model/)
- The feedback process is governed by the E-Heza Executive committee and overseen by the TIP Global Health Steering Committee.
3. Promoting a culture of safety through safe practices and safe systems.
 - E-Heza’s training model is built to encourage co-design and encourages the foundational feedback mechanisms in order to understand both errors of omission and errors of commission. TIP  Global Health takes the following steps to ensure the privacy and security of data collected:
- Healthcare workers sign and commit to a “Protected Health Information Confidentiality Agreement” and receive initial and ongoing training regarding privacy and security.
 - Access to E-Heza’s backend (where private data is held) is secured with role-based permission access and only site administrators with proper need are given access to private data.
- Transfer of data between E-Heza’s front-end client and backend storage is through SSL-encrypted channels only and performed only with authenticated devices.
- E-Heza maintains an access log which tracks all access and both to backend accounts and front end data collection. Weekly audits are performed on the access logs, and the  logs are maintained for one year (and then archived through the prescribed backup retention plan).
- E-Heza’s development operation prohibits the use of non-anonymized data in the development process. No developer may hold personal information on their local system to transfer any personal information from a non-production environment outside the course of the normal backup procedure.
 - E-Heza engages in third-party security audits in order to procure recommendations for further privacy and security procedures.

name: Food Fortification Quality Management System
description: FFQMS is an end-to-end digital solution that ensures quality assurance (QA), quality control (QC), and traceability starting from the procurement of raw material followed by manufacturing of fortified commodities and its storage as well as further distribution across geographies.

sdgRelevance.02: The Food Fortification Quality Management System (FFQMS) plays a pivotal role in addressing malnutrition by ensuring the quality and traceability of fortified foods, directly supporting Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger). Through its comprehensive quality assurance (QA), quality control (QC), and traceability features, the FFQMS ensures that fortified foods meet essential micronutrient standards like Iron, Folic Acid (B9), and Vitamin B12, etc. Aligning with SDG Target 2.2, which aims to eliminate malnutrition by 2030, the FFQMS strengthens fortification processes to fill crucial micro nutritional gaps. Its traceability mechanisms track the journey of raw materials and fortified products from procurement to distribution, ensuring transparency, safety, and accountability across the supply chain. Additionally, the customization feature of FFQMS's validation protocols ensure that fortified foods consistently deliver the required micronutrients, directly contributing to improving public health outcomes. By supporting large-scale food fortification programs, the FFQMS enhances efforts to combat malnutrition and ensures that vulnerable populations receive nutritionally adequate food. In this way, the system plays a critical role in advancing global efforts to end hunger and achieve sustainable food security for all.

openAlternatives: The project currently uses immudb, a tamper-evident database that is source-available under the Business Source License (BSL). We are currently using version 1.5 of immudb, which is licensed under Apache 2.0 and was the stable open-source release available at this time. This version incorporates fixes for all known security vulnerabilities, and as of now, there have been no issues or reported problems with the integration, and the application continues to function as expected. We remain committed to transitioning to an alternative if any security risks arise or if future enhancements necessitate the change. While our current implementation uses immudb for tamper-evident logging, a possible alternative could be implemented using PostgreSQL with cryptographic hashing (e.g., SHA-256). In this approach, each audit entry includes a hash of the row’s own contents (such as action, actor, timestamp, and data). These hashes are generated within the system, and the keys used for hashing are not exposed externally, ensuring that any unauthorized modification to the data would result in a hash mismatch during verification. While updates to the audit log are technically possible, they can only be performed through the controlled system logic, preserving the integrity of the log. This method may suit projects looking for a simple, transparent, and fully open-source alternative to immudb. For the ease of the users to use PostreSQL as an alternative to immudb, a pull request that consists of a markdown file with description and code snippets is available at - https://github.com/Food-Fortification/Food-Fortification-Quality-Management-System/pull/8
nonPIINotes: The Food Fortification Quality Management System allows users (as per their role) to export only their own non-PII and aggregated data in Excel format. It also enables system administrator to upload non-PII data in Excel format through the REST API, ensuring smooth data handling and integration.
privacyNotes: Food Fortification Quality Management System complies with the Indian IT Act, including the Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information - SPDI) Rules, 2011, which define SPDI and mandate consent and privacy policies, the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2023,India, which establishes a Data Protection Authority and aligns with global standards, and the Information Technology Act, 2000, India (amended in 2008), which imposes obligations on protecting sensitive data and penalties for negligence.
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
HTTPS/SSL (encrypted connections to the app are automatically forwarded and enforced), OAuth2/OIDC/JWT (FFQMS uses Keycloak for Identity Access Management, following these security protocols), OpenAPI (backend services provide API documentation in standard format, e.g., https://food-api.fortification.in/iam/swagger-ui/index.html), BPMN 2.0 (workflow processes and user actions are configured using BPMN 2.0 in the system), PDF (test reports and documents are uploaded in PDF format), Excel (aggregate data exports are available in Excel format), WebSocket (user-triggered events are encrypted and broadcast to registered subscribers via WebSocket). 

The Food Fortification Quality Management System adheres to the Principles for Digital Development (Information and Communication Technology for Development - ICT4D) throughout its design, development, and implementation. These principles serve as the foundation of the system, guiding every stage of the work. The system is developed following best practices within the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), ensuring the implementation of version control mechanisms for effective change management. Agile development methodologies are deeply embedded in the process, allowing for iterative development and continuous user feedback. This helps the system to evolve and improve over time while meeting user needs effectively. The software architecture is built with a strong emphasis on modularity, maintainability, and security. It leverages widely adopted frameworks based on free and open-source software, ensuring longevity, easy updates, and compliance with established web standards. The microservices-based architecture, grounded in SOLID principles (Single Responsibility, Open-Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion), enables services to be modular and independently deployable. This ensures scalability, reusability, and extensibility, while the use of containerization technologies like Docker supports independent deployment of backend services, making it easier to set up, maintain, and scale the system. As the system is designed to handle increasing growth in users, organizations, and transactions without performance degradation, scalability is central to the architecture. This ensures that the system can expand efficiently without compromising performance. Security is a priority at every level, with strong mechanisms for authentication, authorization, encryption (TLS/SSL). Regular audits and adherence to OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project) security practices ensure the highest level of data protection, including enforced password complexity and multi-layered security protocols, keeping sensitive data secure and compliant with industry standards. The system also ensures data integrity, maintaining consistency and accuracy across operations, thus avoiding data corruption or discrepancies. It incorporates auditability features that log and maintain a detailed history of changes and interactions, providing full traceability and accountability for all actions taken within the system. Users can also easily export data in Excel format, making the system flexible and data accessible for analysis or reporting purposes. The system supports real-time tracking, operational status, and status changes, which is crucial for seamless monitoring and decision-making. Furthermore, it includes provisions for data retention, ensuring that all logs and audit trails are stored securely for compliance and long-term storage needs. The System’s use of containerization via Docker enables independent deployment of backend services, further simplifying the system’s setup and maintenance. With all these features, the Food Fortification Quality Management System ensures it remains scalable, secure, interoperable, and aligned with global best practices for digital development. This comprehensive approach, which encompasses modularity, security, scalability, maintainability, and future-proofing, makes the Food Fortification Quality Management System an adaptable and robust system capable of supporting evolving user needs while adhering to the highest standards of digital and software development.

name: FUSS - Free Upgrade for a digitally Sustainable School
description: FUSS is a complete GNU/Linux solution based on Debian and around 200 educational software packages for schools. It is a project that allows students and teachers to use at home the same tools installed at school, freely and without any cost to families.

sdgRelevance.04:
[SDG 4] Bringing GNU/Linux and free educational software via the FUSS Project in schools contributes significantly to fulfilling Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) in several ways:
1. Accessible and inclusive education: FOSS (Free Open Source Software) provides free access to high-quality educational resources, tools, and platforms, ensuring that students from all backgrounds can access educational materials and opportunities. This helps bridge the digital divide and promote inclusivity in education.
2. Cost-effective solutions: FOSS is often free or available at a low cost, which reduces the financial burden on educational institutions. This allows schools to allocate their resources more effectively and reach a larger number of students, especially in resource-constrained settings.
3. Collaborative learning: FOSS encourages collaboration and knowledge-sharing among students, teachers, and educational institutions. It enables the creation of online communities where educators can share resources, exchange ideas, and collaborate on the development of educational content. This fosters a culture of collaborative learning and innovation.
4. Customization and adaptability: FOSS software can be customized and adapted to suit the specific needs and context of different schools and educational systems. This flexibility allows teachers to tailor educational content and platforms to meet the diverse learning styles, interests, and capabilities of students, enhancing the quality and relevance of education. In FUSS we adapted the distribution for schools that need specific software e.g. music schools or certain technical schools.
5. Digital literacy and innovation: FOSS software offers opportunities for students to develop digital literacy skills and encourages them to become active creators rather than just technology tourists. By engaging with FOSS projects, students can gain practical experience in coding, software development, and problem-solving. This nurtures their creativity, critical thinking, and innovation, aligning with SDG9's focus on industry and infrastructure development.
6. Support for open educational resources (OER): FOSS software facilitates the creation, sharing, and use of open educational resources (OER). OER are freely accessible and adaptable learning materials that can be shared and reused, allowing educators to access a wide range of high-quality teaching resources. This promotes the use of up-to-date, relevant, and localized educational content, fostering the delivery of quality education.

 [SDG 9] FOSS in schools can play a significant role in fulfilling SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure). Here are some ways in which the FUSS Project and FOSS, in general, can contribute:
1. Cost-effectiveness and accessibility: FOSS software is typically available for free or at low costs, eliminating the need for expensive licenses or ongoing fees. This allows e.g. start-ups that want to work with schools with a FOSS-based business model, to cut initial costs while providing development and maintenance services for schools. This is what happened and happens with Project FUSS where its technological partners helped the project flourish keeping it up-to-date with free modern technologies. One of our technological partners was a student in one of our schools who helped develop the FUSS distribution voluntarily almost daily.
2. Innovation and collaboration: FOSS software encourages collaboration among companies, as it allows users to access, modify, distribute, and exchange the source code freely. In schools, this fosters creativity and innovation by enabling students to experiment, customize, and develop their coding and programming skills which can be spent during compulsory internships in IT companies or public institutions. Through such collaborative practices, FOSS software promotes industry innovation, laying the foundation for future technological advancements.
3. Skill development: By embracing FOSS software, schools can provide students with hands-on experience and practical knowledge of coding, programming, and software development. These skills are highly sought after in the job market and can empower students to pursue careers in industries related to technology and innovation, contributing to the overall growth of the economy.
4. Infrastructure development: FOSS software often requires lower hardware specifications compared to proprietary alternatives, making it more adaptable to different types of infrastructure and devices. This flexibility allows schools to optimize their existing infrastructure and extend the lifespan of their hardware, reducing the need for constant upgrades or replacements. Consequently, FOSS software supports the development and maintenance of sustainable and resilient infrastructure. For years our schools have been using refurbished hardware to save money, and natural resources, and contribute to a circular economy.
5. Localized solutions: FOSS software provides the opportunity for schools and local communities to create and adapt technology solutions to address specific challenges. This empowers educators, students, and local developers to cater to their unique needs and find innovative solutions to problems related to education, infrastructure, or social development. By promoting localized innovation, FOSS software supports the achievement of SDG9 at a grassroots level.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.03: GeoPrism Registry (GPR) is an IT solution that provides a single source of truth for managing geographic data over time across multiple information systems and data sources. It allows for the simultaneous hosting, management, regular update, and sharing of master lists, associated hierarchies, and geospatial data for the geographic objects core to sustainable development including public health, education, agriculture, infrastructure, and other public and private services. SDG 3: GPR manages up-to-date and historical geographic data necessary to identify areas and populations most at risk for natural disasters or other public health emergencies; to ensure universal coverage of health, education, and other services; and to enable allocation of resources to the right places at the right time in a systematic and data-driven way. SDG 13: GPR uses spatial knowledge graphs to integrate interrelated and cross-domain data by geographic objects to help identify gaps in current flood preparedness, calculate cost of flood loss due to downstream impact, and help municipal organizations factor climate change adaptation into their decision-making processes. SDG 16: GPR can store, manage and share information that are official and non-official, actual and historic, regarding the geographic objects key to sustainable development like administrative divisions, villages, infrastructure and other relevant physical and virtual features forming our environment.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.16: We build free open source software to provide modern journalists with the technology needed to run an independent news organisation — from publishing, to distribution, subscriptions, and payments. We believe that sustainable media is vital to sustainable democracy, and our product is designed to help news organisations not just survive, but thrive, within an information ecosystem that's moving faster than ever. To date, our product has generated revenue exceeding $100M for independent publishers, in support of this mission. Target 16.10: Ensure public access to information and protect fundamental freedoms: By offering a platform that is not controlled by centralized algorithms or corporate interests, Ghost protects the freedom of expression and ensures that diverse, independent voices have the tools to provide public access to information.

openAlternatives: Ghost uses several third-party (proprietary/commercial) services. None of them are strictly required to run a basic Ghost site, but some are essential for specific flagship features. [1] Stripe is the exclusive payment processor for paid memberships, subscriptions, and donations. [2] Mailgun is the default built-in bulk email provider, which can be switched to any SMTP provider. [3] Tinybird is a proprietary real-time analytics database used for the Ghost Stats dashboard (page views, traffic sources, top content). It is entirely optional. [4] The Unsplash API is used in the editor to search and insert free stock photos. It is fully optional — it can be disabled via a toggle in admin settings. [5] Tenor (now owned by Google) is used for the GIF card in the editor. It is fully optional. [6] Sentry is used for server-side and frontend error tracking and performance tracing. It is entirely optional. [7] Slack webhooks are used for two optional notification systems. [8] Optional AWS S3-compatible adapter.

name: Go.Data
description: Go.Data is an open-source platform for outbreak response and contact tracing developed by WHO in collaboration with GOARN partners. It streamlines all aspects of outbreak response and is highly versatile with customizable configurations for different scenarios.

sdgs.name: SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth

sdgRelevance.03: SDG 3 - Good Health and Well-being: SDG Target 3.3 | End the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and neglected tropical diseases and combat hepatitis, water-borne diseases and other communicable diseases. Relevance: Go.Data addresses this target by providing real-time data and analytics to quickly identify, monitor, and control outbreaks of infectious diseases. This helps reduce their spread and impact. SDG Target 3.8 | Achieve universal health coverage, including financial risk protection, access to quality essential healthcare services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all Relevance: The Go.Data tool can enhance health systems' ability to respond effectively to disease outbreaks, ensuring that healthcare services are not overwhelmed and that infected people can access essential healthcare services during outbreaks. SDG 6 - Clean Water and Sanitation: Target 6.1 | By 2030, achieve universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all. Relevance: Go.Data can be used to control water-borne diseases, ensuring safe drinking water supplies. Early detection and response to water contamination-related outbreaks help maintain safe access to drinking water. SDG 8 - Decent Work and Economic Growth Target 8.8 | Protect labor rights and promote safe and secure working environments for all workers, including migrant workers, in particular women migrants, and those in precarious employment. Relevance: By effectively controlling outbreaks, Go.Data supports maintaining healthy working environments and preventing economic disruptions caused by widespread illness, thus contributing to economic stability and the protection of workers' health. SDG 11 - Sustainable Cities and Communities Target 11.5 | By 2030, significantly reduce the number of deaths and the number of people affected and substantially decrease the direct economic losses relative to the global gross domestic product caused by disasters, including water-related disasters, with a focus on protecting the poor and people in vulnerable situations. Relevance: Go.Data contributes to minimizing the impact of health emergencies on communities, particularly vulnerable populations. Rapid and effective outbreak response helps reduce health-related deaths, and economic losses and protects the most vulnerable. In conclusion, Go.Data is a powerful tool that contributes to multiple SDGs. Its capacity to improve the prompt detection, monitoring, and management of disease outbreaks contributes to building resilient health systems, promoting community safety, and enhancing overall well-being. By directly addressing health emergencies, this tool also contributes to broader objectives of sustainable development, such as ensuring economic stability, facilitating access to clean water, providing safe working environments, and strengthening data infrastructure.

openAlternatives: Go.Data works with MongoDB because of its extensive features and flexibility. However, it is possible to use a fully Open-source alternative such as FerretDB. Detailed instructions for migrating from MongoDB to FerretDB can be found at: https://github.com/WorldHealthOrganization/GoDataSource-Installers/blob/main/docs/configuring-ferret-db.md
nonPIINotes: Go.Data is designed to capture identifiable data for cases and contacts, facilitating their effective identification, follow-up, and implementation of control measures. Nevertheless, the software provides an array of functionalities to export this data in a non-PII format. Specifically, the application enables exporting cases and contacts data, including their related data such as laboratory and hospitalization, in the following formats: CSV, XML, JSON, ODS, and PDF. During the data export, the user has the option to select all the variables that will be anonymized in the exported data set.

• Architecture Principles: - Free and Open-Source Software (FOSS): Go.Data is developed as FOSS, ensuring transparency and collaborative improvement (https://github.com/WorldHealthOrganization/godata). - Integrations and extensions: Go.Data has extensive documentation and tools for integrating and extending Go.Data (https://worldhealthorganization.github.io/godata/integration/). - ICT4D principles: Go.Data development approach aligns with ICT for Development principles (https://github.com/WorldHealthOrganization/godata/blob/master/docs/ index.md). - Principles for digital development: Go.Data adheres to these principles, focusing on user-centricity, scalability, sustainability, and data security. • User interface/user experience (UI/UX) - Human-centered design principles: The Go.Data design approach prioritizes the needs and experiences of users, ensuring intuitive and accessible interfaces. - Material design: The Go.Data project follows material design guidelines to create visually appealing and consistent user interfaces. • Coding styles & standards: - Open-source compliance: Go.Data adhere to the WHO Open Source Programme, promoting transparency and community collaboration (https://github.com/topics/open- source; https://github.com/WorldHealthOrganization/godata). • Security Best Practices: - User authentication and authorization: Go.Data supports the creation of strong passwords for username/ password authentication. In addition, end-users can enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and manage resource access authorization through access control rights/permissions. - IT auditing and data protection: To protect data at rest, Go.Data employs data encryption, firewalls, antivirus protection, and scheduled backups to secure data. To protect data in transit, Go.Data ensures data integrity and security using TLS/SSL encryption and X.509 certificates for remote authentication
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity: Go.Data has undergone multiple security audits with the assistance of WHO cybersecurity and a member state. These audits involved a combination of automated and manual tests, including ethical hacking. The following is a list of details related to the security of Go.Data: • Sensitive data like passwords are hashed. • Captcha can be optionally enabled on password-related screens. (Captcha feature is included in the Go.Data application and can be optionally activated to challenge the user at login, password reset email request, and the resetting of the password) • Two-factor authentication can be enabled on password-related screens. This proceeds via the dispatch of an email so a working SMTP server must be configured with Go.Data. • Brute force handling: This is used to disable reset passwords with question & answers for a time for a specific user after a defined number of incorrect password attempts. Account lockouts can last a specific duration as defined in the config.json file fragment below. • "bruteForce": { "resetPassword": { "enabled": false, "maxRetries": 10, "resetTime": 30, "resetTimeUnit": "minutes" • Authentication tokens: This property in the config.json file dictates the behavior regarding authentication tokens and whether these are invalidated by a restart of the Go.Data service. When set to false, a Go.Data server restart does not log out any active sessions and their tokens remain valid. When set to true, a restart of the Go.Data server destroys tokens so that users will need to log back in. "signoutUsersOnRestart": false, • All backups can be encrypted by specifying the encryption key in config.json file: "backUp": { "password": "key" (Without this encryption key backup restore will fail for backups encrypted with this key, therefore do not misplace it.) } • Communication between mobile apps and API can be encrypted as well: Users have the option to exchange encrypted information between the app and the API. This option is present on the hub configuration screen as the “Encrypted connection” switch. By default, the encrypted connection is turned on. This option can later be turned off from the hub configuration screen. Go.Data is considered sufficiently hardened for common cybersecurity attacks provided that the configurable features such as CORS, multi-factor authentication, and token timeouts are set correctly. The environment in which Go.Data is deployed must also be validated to ensure that there are no vulnerabilities.
contentManagement: Content is NOT collected NOT stored and NOT distributed.
harrassmentPolicy: Go.Data adheres to the WHO policies and codes of conduct for Preventing and Responding to Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment (https://www.who.int/initiatives/preventing-and-responding-to-sexual-exploitation-abuse-and-harassment). These policies and codes are also reflected in the application's code of conduct for members, contributors, and leaders within the Go.Data community (https://github.com/WorldHealthOrganization/godata/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

name: Harmony
description: Harmony is an open-source, end-to end data integration and advanced analytics platform for integrating, harmonizing, analyzing, and visualizing any number of structured data sources from different sectors (e.g. health, education, agriculture, sustainable development, climate change adaptation), ranging from routinely collected individual level data to operational research and survey data.

sdgs.name: SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere
SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth

sdgRelevance.01:
Harmony currently serves as the open source, data integration, and data analytics platform for governments in 8 low-, middle- and upper-middle-income countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. It is also used by the RBM Partnership to End Malaria for global coordination of the malaria response. Scaled through funding by the Global Fund, GAVI, USAID, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Big Win Philanthropy, Vital Strategies, and the Pan American Health Organization, Harmony is utilized to integrate and analyze data across various sectors, including health (for national and sub-national HIV, TB, Malaria, supply chain, programs) and poverty reduction.  Harmony has been used to integrate data from multiple structured data sources, including various health management information systems (e.g. DHIS2), logistic management information systems (e.g. OpenLMIS), Excel and CSV files, surveys (e.g. Demographic and Health Surveys), scorecards, financial data, from individual-level data to national surveys, and from open source and enterprise systems. Once data is integrated, it is used to optimize vaccine supply chains, improve financial and human resource allocations for health programs, mitigate the loss to follow-up of patients, identify and respond to data quality issues, align labor data to educational supply data, rapidly respond to global or national emergencies (e.g. hurricanes and pandemics), and coordinate inter-agency actions and funding.

SDG 1. No Poverty Evidence: Harmony is being deployed in more than 8 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and in more than 25 countries through global projects, to integrate and effectively utilize data to mitigate the health and economic challenges felt by those living in extreme poverty. Harmony supports a myriad of governments and organizations to focus on health poverty alleviation that leads to improved health outcomes, a reduction in out-of-pocket payments and health expenditures, and a healthier workforce. For example, through the RBM Partnership to End Malaria project, Zenysis is supporting the development coordination, and mobilization of resources from a variety of sources, in order to provide an adequate and predictable supply of malaria commodities and technical assistance services that impact those living in extreme poverty.  Every country Harmony is deployed in is classified as low or middle-income country per the World Bank’s classification.   ,

SDG 3. Good Health and Well-being Evidence: Harmony is utilized to integrate and analyze data across various disease areas within the health sector, including but not limited to, national and sub-national HIV, TB, and Malaria programs. Harmony has been used to integrate data from multiple structured data sources, including various health management information systems (e.g. DHIS2), logistic management information systems (e.g. OpenLMIS), Excel and CSV files, surveys (e.g. Demographic and Health Surveys), scorecards, financial data, from individual-level data to national surveys, and from open source and enterprise systems. Once data has been integrated, it is being used to optimize vaccine supply chains, improve financial and human resource allocations for health programs, mitigate loss to follow up of patients, identify and respond to data quality issues, align labor data to educational supply data, rapidly respond to global or national emergencies (e.g. hurricanes and pandemics), and coordinate inter-agency actions and funding. Harmony is used by national health ministries, global health stakeholders (The Global Fund, Gavi, USAID). During the COVID-19 pandemic, 3 countries utilized their instance of Harmony for their pandemic response. Excerpt from Devex Article: “Zenysis builds relationships by starting small, and solving data and interoperability problems, identified by users,” John Fairhurst, the head of private sector engagement at the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, told Devex by email. “This model has proved effective in a range of operating and digital maturity contexts." In addition to Mozambique, Zenysis works in Brazil, Pakistan, South Africa, Zambia, Benin, Ethiopia, and Rwanda, as well as for the RBM Partnership to End Malaria, which operates globally. Rwanda Biomedical Centre, a government organization affiliated with Rwanda’s Health Ministry, used to have separate tracking systems for different health priorities, with one for HIV/AIDS, another for malaria, another for tuberculosis, and so on. It is now partnering with Zenysis, which is working on a new agreement with the Rwandan government. RBC said Zenysis’ approach is different from those of other tech companies that have come and gone over the years. “We attribute most of those failures to a lack of ownership or long-term vision,” said Albert Tuyishime, division manager for planning, business strategy, and monitoring and evaluation at RBC. “We’ve had some partners pull out, saying: ‘Our time here has elapsed. The resources we had are now finished, so we have to step out.’” ,

SDG 5. Gender Equality Evidence: In all deployments, where sex or gender disaggregated data is available, Harmony collects and integrates data on gender that can then be disaggregated and analyzed to help the government unlock key insights to have an impact on the gender-specific outcomes. For example, in South Africa, Zenysis’ software was used for the integration of Adolescent Girls and Young Women programmatic data across three Global Fund stakeholders. By using Zenysis’ analytics tools, the stakeholders have enhanced capacity to track cohorts of clients through time for their respective programs and refer clients more effectively to external services. Excerpt from Global Fund Overview Publication: “In public health programming we need to be a lot smarter in the way we use data in order to make the money go further and ensure that we reach the communities we are trying to reach with the services they require at the right time. NACOSA previously used a spreadsheet to track the number of sex workers reached in South Africa and it became very difficult to accurately track the types of services received and the profiles of the sex workers that we reached. With the Zenysis data platform we are now able to look at the unique number of sex workers reached and the exact services provided. We are able to analyse the data down to a hotspot level to be able to tailor programmatic interventions to better reach the sex workers at the right times. Additionally, we have been able to merge programmatic and finance data, which has helped us look at the cost-effectiveness of the program and identify problems.” Leora Casey Key Populations Manager, Networking HIV & AIDS Community of Southern Africa (NACOSA),

SDG 6. Clean Water and Sanitation Evidence: Harmony can be used to integrate a myriad of cross-sectoral data systems that can be utilized for analysis. For example data on water quality can be integrated with health data, infrastructure data, and supply chain data to pinpoint an outbreak due to unclean water and optimize the delivery of health commodities to that location.  In March and April 2019, Tropical Cyclones Idai and Kenneth made landfall in Mozambique. The National Institute of Health of Mozambique used Harmony to quickly integrate 8 separate critical emergency response systems into a single platform for analysis. By analyzing the data integrated within Harmony and optimizing key interventions, the Government and all of its partners, including the World Health Organization and Doctors Without Borders, were able to identify tainted water sources and subsequently reduce the number of new cholera cases in Sofala Province, where Cyclone Idai made landfall, from over four hundred (400) per day to zero (0). Excerpt from FT Article: Zenysis formed part of a “virtual control room”, integrating information to help decision makers understand what was happening in the worst hit areas, identify sources of water contamination and where to prioritise cholera vaccinations. It supported an “mAlert system”, which integrated health surveillance data into a single platform for analysis. The output was daily reports distilled from data issued by health facilities and accommodation centres in affected areas, disease monitoring and surveillance from laboratory testing. Machine learning applied to disparate data helps manage shortages of medical supplies Eduardo Samo Gudo, deputy director-general of Mozambique’s National Health Institute, says that such information, combined with epidemiological bulletins and detailed presentations, helped inform daily discussions and decisions.,

SDG 8. Decent Work and Economic Growth Evidence: Zenysis is working with the Jobs Creation Commission (JCC) to establish a Jobs Enablement and Data Interoperability (JEDI) platform to help the government manage and monitor its job creation programs. The platform, supported by Big Win Philanthropy, brings together a number of data sources to generate insights for policymakers, employers, job seekers and employment agencies.  Excerpt from Big Win Philanthropy Article: During this meeting, the delegation also learned about Ethiopia’s Jobs Enablement and Data Interoperability (JEDI) platform, developed by Zenysis Technologies to facilitate evidence-based decision-making through aggregating employment data from different information systems. Now in its second phase of expansion, the platform aggregates more than 20 data sources including job creation reports, education data, and labor force and employment surveys to create a national employment database and verify the accuracy of reports received from a variety of sources.,

SDG 17. Partnerships for the Goals Evidence: The integration of data across multiple once siloed systems supports the partnership and coordination of both domestic and international stakeholders in each Harmony deployment. For example, the RBM Partnership to End Malaria is the largest global platform for coordinated action towards a world free from malaria and since July 2019, Zenysis Technologies has been working with the RBM partnership to enhance data sharing, coordination and action in the fight against malaria. Zenysis has developed the Global Malaria Monitoring Dashboard to strengthen regional and global reporting requirements, integrate data from different systems, and improve data visualization and management tools. The dashboards integrate epidemiological, programmatic, financial, supply chain, and other data from more than 30 countries.

collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
The user account data is used to create and administer user accounts on the Harmony platform. All user passwords are hashed and salted with the BCrypt password algorithm. This means that Zenysis cannot view passwords created by users of the Harmony project. No user account data is shared with third parties.

Harmony comes with various guidelines, protocols, and tools to help prevent risks and ultimately avoid harm. For example, as noted above, all communication between users of the Harmony platform and the server is encrypted with TLS, Harmony servers should support TLS 1.3, the use of Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) and Elliptic Curve Cryptography ensures that no Protected Data will leave servers in an unencrypted state, and protected Data stored on configured servers is encrypted with Advanced Encryption Standard 128 (AES-128).   Furthermore, at the user level, unique identifiers and passwords are given to each user with specific accessibility guardrails that are defined by key stakeholders overseeing any instance of Harmony. Users are also automatically logged out of their user session after 30 minutes of inactivity by default. Given Harmony is open source and may be used freely, if Zenysis is not supporting the Harmony implementation/utilization, we expect organizations to also establish their own data and privacy risk mitigation efforts, beyond what is already offered in the software, in accordance with any applicable local laws or best practices. All communication between users of the Harmony platform and the server is encrypted with TLS. Harmony servers should support TLS 1.3, the use of Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) and Elliptic Curve Cryptography ensures that no Protected Data will leave servers in an unencrypted state, and protected Data stored on configured servers is encrypted with Advanced Encryption Standard 128 (AES-128)

The configuration of the platform is flexible and administrators are able to adjust how the platform operates to abide by local laws and requirements. For example, access to Protected Data at the indicator level, dashboards, analyses, and other functionality can be delegated on a per-user basis. Harmony administrators are responsible for determining the appropriate levels of access each user shall have. In addition, data can be encrypted in transit as well as at rest.

harrassmentPolicy:
Harmony's Code of Conduct can be found here: https://github.com/Zenysis/Harmony?tab=coc-ov-file#readme

Currently Harmony contributors and users interact through Zenysis' facilitation. E.g. A country's Information and Communications Technology (ICT) manager may want a new feature in Harmony, which is discussed and supported through Zenysis' engineering and product teams. Thus, at this time, any user that interacts with a contributor is known to Zenysis and does not include underage users. Users also have the ability to connect with Zenysis staff through various channels (in-platform, email, in-person, phone etc) in country or globally, if the user finds any issues utilizing our software or when dealing with contributors or when building the software.

Furthermore, as noted above, access to data at the indicator level, dashboards, analyses, and other functionality can be delegated on a per-user basis. Harmony administrators are responsible for determining the appropriate levels of access each user shall have. Thus, access is established by administrators who target only professional users and also would be responsible for flagging, addressing, and taking any action necessary to project users.

In the future, Zenysis will plan to have a Harmony Community of Practice, which will include age limits for participation and community guidelines that provide a code of conduct and governance for the community. The Zenysis team will create both automated and non-automated processes to flag inappropriate behavior, risk, harassment or any other deleterious actions or posts by users or contributors.

name: Health Claims Data Exchange
description: The HCX Platform by Swasth Alliance enables seamless health claims data exchange with tools like SDKs, management apps, and an exchange switch—boosting collaboration and interoperability across the health ecosystem.

sdgRelevance.03: The HCX Platform directly contributes to SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) by enhancing the efficiency and transparency of the health claims process. Through seamless data exchange, the platform enables effective collaboration between healthcare providers and insurers, reducing both the time and cost associated with claims processing. It improves access to quality healthcare by ensuring both syntactic and semantic interoperability across the ecosystem. By lowering administrative costs and increasing operational efficiency, the platform supports the achievement of universal health coverage (UHC). The HCX Platform also aligns with SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) by providing an interoperable digital infrastructure for the secure exchange of health data. Designed for scalability, the platform supports innovative healthcare delivery models and fosters trust and collaboration between public and private health entities.

nonPIINotes: The running instance of HCX Platform stores essential non-PII data in two main areas: 1. HCX Registries: Information about participating organisations, including unique identifiers and metadata, is stored within HCX registries. These registries enable streamlined data exchange and routing, ensuring accurate identification and communication between participants. Details on the content of registry are available at - https://docs.hcxprotocol.io/hcx-technical-specifications/open-protocol/registries 2. Message Headers: Non-PII information in message headers is also stored, facilitating secure and efficient message routing, validation, and processing across the platform. Details on the content of Message Headers are available at - https://docs.hcxprotocol.io/hcx-technical-specifications/open-protocol/key-components-building-blocks/message-structure
privacyNotes: The HCX Platform strictly follows the security and privacy norms set by the HCX Protocol and is designed to comply with key data protection regulations, including: - India’s Personal Data Protection Bill (2019). - The Information Technology Act (2000). - Global data protection regulations, such as GDPR (where applicable). With its modular and adaptable architecture, the HCX Platform can be readily configured to meet additional local data protection laws and regulations, ensuring ongoing compliance as these laws evolve.
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
The HCX Platform adheres to the following open standards, ensuring secure, interoperable, and high-performance data exchanges: - Security Protocols: HTTPS, SSL, SSH, RS256, ED2556, and AnonCreds. - Authentication & Authorization: OAuth 2, OID4VC, OID4VP, OIDC, and JWT (JSON Web Tokens). - Interoperability Standards: FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), HL7 (Health Level 7), and OpenAPI 3.0. 

The HCX Platform aligns with the following industry best practices to promote security, reliability, and scalability: - Data Security by Design: Encryption for data in transit and at rest, with security embedded at every protocol layer. - Modularity and Scalability: A microservices architecture ensures each component can be independently scaled or modified as needed, allowing flexible adaptation to growing ecosystem demands. - Transparency and Interoperability: The platform’s use of FHIR standards and OpenAPI specifications facilitates seamless data exchange, supporting ecosystem-wide interoperability. - Community-Driven Development: Contributions from the open community, including SDKs and other tools, enhance extensibility and foster collaborative innovation within the ecosystem.
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
In a live HCX Platform instance, PII data is only collected for operational users from the HCX switch operator and participating organizations. These users act as points of contact for their respective organizations and configure secure routing of claims messages to their designated endpoints. Collected PII includes: - User name - Email ID - Mobile number - Associated participant details.

The HCX Platform is designed with data privacy and security as foundational principles, fully aligned with the HCX Protocol’s stringent standards: - Access Control: The platform utilizes Keycloak for managing user credentials and roles, supporting role-based access and secure authentication. - Encryption: Basic PII, such as usernames, emails, and hashed passwords, is stored securely, with encryption applied at the database level. Data in transit is protected using industry-standard encryption protocols, including HTTPS and SSL. - Auditability: The platform includes logging and audit trails to track access and modifications, ensuring accountability and transparency.
contentManagement: Content is NOT collected NOT stored and NOT distributed.
harrassmentPolicy: The HCX Platform fosters collaboration among operational users and community members. Interactions between contributors are governed by a Code of Conduct, adapted from GitHub Community guidelines, ensuring respectful and safe collaboration. This Code of Conduct supports a safe and inclusive environment, allowing all participants to engage constructively and responsibly. https://hcxprotocol.io/community/ In a live instance of HCX, interactions between users are also governed by local regulatory authorities, such as the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). name: IASO
description: IASO is an innovative, open-source, bilingual (EN/FR) data collection platform with advanced geospatial features to plan, monitor and evaluate health, environmental or social programmes. Main features: geo-enabled data collection, georegistry, microplanning, entities & workflows.

sdgRelevance.02:
SDG2: IASO is the underlying open source software to an UN nutrition program solution for beneficiary tracking.

SDG 3: IASO has become a trusted name for health data management with implementations in 12 countries and two large-scale multi-country projects, in support to the Global Polio Eradication Initiative and an UN nutrition program solution. Main projects range from health systems PBF (Performance Based Financing) schemes data collection, georegistries, health maps update, geo-enabled microplanning as well as end-to-end health campaigns digitalization.

SDG4: IASO was used to locate schools and collect key data about each of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

nonPIINotes: All data, including non PII data, can be exported to CSV and XLSX format, or through an API in json format. On top of that, the system allows the collection of geographical information (about, for example, health facilities location) and can import data either directly from DHIS2 API, in CSV, or in the standard geopackage format (https://www.geopackage.org/). Exporting is possible in all these formats too.
privacyNotes: IASO can totally be used in a GDPR compliant fashion. Users can be kept anonymous, data collections can be designed either to not collect any PII, or to ask for consent for each data collection. In terms of security, it supports having data securely saved, transfer of data over secure connections, passwords stored in hashed format. A lot of these features are inherited from the Django development framework on which Iaso is built. That said, as would be the case for, e.g., database software, nothing can ensure that the software users will not use the software in a non GDPR compliant way. Ultimately, it is the responsibility of the implementer / project manager to ensure compliance with GDPR.
bestPractices: Scalability and Performance/ Scaling and Optimization
standardsAndPracticesNotes: We can account with the following principles for digital development: Design with User - Our software is designed in perpetual feedback loop with users, where most features tend to be mocked up and shown to end users before being implemented to allow to spot hard to understand concept, security and access issues and such.  Understand the Existing Ecosystem - Iaso integrates with the existing ecosystem. In particular, it allows to reuse forms in the common xlsform format and to import and export data to DHIS2, which is probably the most installed health information management system. In terms of data collection, Iaso differentiate itself from other data collection tools by being offline-first, ensuring that data collection can happen even when no internet connectivity is available. Design for Scale - Performance is at the center of our work as, for cost effectiveness, we try to host multiple customers on the same servers, while still providing a quality experience to each customer individually. This leads us to constantly monitor performance. Outside of the performance issue, Iaso is also designed to split the work of various teams in sub teams, or to limit access by geographical scope, which allows sometimes thousands of people to collaborate on the same data collection effort without conflicting results. Build for Sustainability - We rely on open source software components and are building a solution that organizations can install and manage locally.  Reuse and Improve - We have reused lots of various open source products, and amongst them, the ODK project, which is a Digital Public Good. IASO also had bidirectional integration with DHIS2, the reference Health Management System in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), enabling users to import or expert data from/to IASO as needed.
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
This is a generic data collection platform used in health system. It's possible to collect personal information both on patients/beneficiaries and workers using the system.

The project has a strong focus on security of the data stored, on restricting access to data to only the authorized users, based on their geographical and managerial features, in the goal of avoiding doing harm to end users by letting their data be communicated outside of the scope they intended it for. The project also features lots of traceability features, allowing to understand where changes to data are coming from and detect potential abuse.  Finally, by focussing on open formats, the project aims at keeping the collected data usable outside of Iaso, so that efforts invested in the software are not lost if in the future the development is discontinued. All data collection efforts are benefiting from password protection. Data access is segmented and access to the data collection interfaces does not mean access to all the data collected in underlying efforts. Passwords are encrypted and all traffic to non secure http are redirected to https.  The software is hostable locally, which allows it to observe local data storage laws for patient/beneficiary data.

name: IVTToken
description: This initiative connects under connected schools to the internet through a blockchain model, rewarding ISPs and sponsors with connectivity tokens. Supported by UNICEF, it focuses on usability and scalability to enhance global educational access.

sdgRelevance.04:
SDG 4: Quality Education
IVTToken directly contributes to achieving inclusive and equitable quality education by enhancing access to learning opportunities through internet connectivity. By connecting schools in under-connected areas, we are helping bridge the educational divide, aligning with SDG 4's targets of ensuring equal access to all levels of education and promoting lifelong learning opportunities.

SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure
The use of blockchain technology in our solution supports the development of sustainable and resilient infrastructure, promoting inclusive and sustainable industrialization. This aligns with SDG 9's targets of building resilient infrastructure and fostering innovation, especially in terms of increasing access to information and communications technology.

SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals
Our approach of collaborating with ISPs, governments, and international organizations exemplifies the spirit of SDG 17, which emphasizes the importance of multi-stakeholder partnerships. These collaborations are crucial for mobilizing and sharing knowledge, expertise, technology, and financial resources, all of which are essential for achieving all the SDGs.
