name: Syft
description: Syft allows external researchers to securely conduct remote data science while protecting privacy, security, and intellectual property.

sdgRelevance.09: Syft allows researchers to get answers hidden in private or sensitive data without making a copy or allowing direct access, potentially unlocking 1000x more data in every scientific field. Syft thus provides data infrastructure that supports SDG 9, in particular Target 9.5 to “enhance research and upgrade industrial technologies”. More broadly, Syft can enable data access that has cross-cutting impact across all SDGs. Such interventions are captured by SDG17, to “strengthen the means of implementation” of the other SDGs. Target 17.16 is to “mobilize and share knowledge, expertise, technology”, and Target 17.17 is to “encourage and promote effective public, public-private and civil society partnerships”. Syft lowers the barriers to such partnerships by resolving concerns around data privacy, security and intellectual property, enabling organisations to more easily collaborate and share information in support of the SDGs.

nonPIINotes: Syft enables data owners to import their data assets into a Syft Datasite, which is hosted within the data owner’s computing environment. Syft supports blob storage, meaning information assets can be loaded in any format, and can be hosted either locally or via a cloud service. Assets can either be imported directly to the datasite (i.e. copied to the datasite server’s hard drive) or mounted externally to minimise data movement. Data scientists using Syft's cannot extract the raw data from a datasite, but can extract the results of analysis run against that data according to policies determined by the data owner, and enforced through Syft. OpenMined does not collect any data from Syft datasites, nor does it have access to such data. Only the data owner has access to their datasite server
privacyNotes:
Syft is infrastructure that may be deployed and used by data owners and provides privacy and governance mechanisms that can support compliance with a data owner’s usage policies and relevant privacy regulations such as GDPR or the US Privacy Act. We have unlocked sensitive user data in places such as Microsoft and GDPR-protected data in areas such as Dailymotion through our partnership with the Christchurch Call Initiative on Algorithmic Outcomes, where external data scientists could perform research on production AI recommender models.

https://openmined.org/privacy-policy/, https://openmined.org/faqs/
standardsAndPracticesNotes:
OAuth 2 for authentication, OpenAPI 2.0 standard via Traefik reverse proxy,y AES for at-rest encryption.

PySyft is fully open-source software, with over ~25k commits from 100+ individuals located around the world. Development of PySyft utilizes and/or adheres to the following best practices and principles: SDLC: - User stories - Change management using version control - Test driven development using automated tests - Continuous Integration & Continous Deployment (CI/CD) - Code review - Code refactoring Architectural design: - Modularity and Maintainability - Reusability and Extensibility - Accountability & Non-repudiability - Security & Consented Access - Universal Access & Open APIs - Microservices architecture Software architecture styles: - Asynchronous messaging - Peer-to-peer - Client-server Cloud computing: - Best practices on Azure, Google Cloud and AWS Security: - SBOM/code scanning of full software stack
collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
The name and email address of users of a Syft datasite are stored for authentication and authorization purposes - this includes the data owners and any researchers/data scientists. Arbitrary PII data may also be stored in a Syft datasite at the data owner’s discretion and managed according to the data owner’s policies.

Syft provides a data owner with complete control over the data in their datasite - private data never leaves the datasite without the data owner’s explicit permission. Moreover, data owners can impose custom policies that constrain the types of analysis data scientists can run, and can require certain privacy techniques to be applied to results, for example, requiring the implementation of differential privacy. These policies are enforced automatically through software, providing robust data governance. Syft also provides role-based access controls, meaning users require explicit permissions to be enabled on their account in order to access the datasite.

Access to data and content needs to be approved by the owner of the datasite. Inappropriate and illegal content is handled by the data owner that is using Syft, and is managed according to their own policies.
harrassmentPolicy: Contributors to the Syft codebase are required to adhere to the following code of conduct​​: https://github.com/OpenMined/PySyft?tab=coc-ov-file#readme Data owners have full control over who can access their datasite. Data owners may revoke access for users who do not adhere to these policies. Likewise, external researchers have the freedom to choose which datasites they apply to join, and to leave any they have already joined.

nonPIINotes: https://landportal.org/developers/lod-process The process of offering all Land Portal data as Linked Open Data (LOD) involves several steps: 1 Generating RDF from Statistical Data Statistical data, sourced from diverse datasets in various formats (Excel, CSV, APIs, JSON, XML, etc.), is processed using landbook-importers (available on GitHub). These tools convert the data into RDF files that align with the Land Book LOD Data Model. Once generated, these RDF files are ready to be uploaded to the triple store. 2 Uploading RDF Files to Virtuoso The generated RDF files, which contain statistical data, are uploaded to Virtuoso, an RDF triple store. Virtuoso allows the data to be queried using the SPARQL protocol, making it accessible as Linked Open Data. 3 Publishing Data from landportal.org to Virtuoso Data from landportal.org, which is hosted on a Drupal instance and stored in a MySQL database, is also integrated into the Virtuoso triple store. This is achieved using a customized process that combines: 4 A fork of the rdfx module to shape RDF generated by Drupal. A fork of the RDF Drupal Indexer module, which uses Drupal’s Search API to publish RDF triples to the triple store within specific graphs, using the SPARQL Update protocol. Once all the data is available in Virtuoso, it can be queried through the SPARQL endpoint: http://landportal.org/sparql

This principle emphasizes the use of terms from shared, preferably standardized, vocabularies to encode data and metadata, fostering a self-sustaining ecosystem. Bibliographic and Content Model integrates controlled vocabularies developed by the Land Portal alongside the following vocabularies: -Dublin Core: For general resource properties. -Bibliographic Ontology: For specialized bibliographic resource properties. -FOAF Vocabulary: For describing entities such as persons and organizations. -Schema.org Vocabulary: For properties of relevant entities. -SKOS Vocabulary: For related concepts and classifications. Data Storage -The data storage model incorporates the following standardized vocabularies and identifiers: -ISO 8601: For dates and timestamps (yyyy-mm-dd). -ISBN/ISSN/DOI/Handle: For unique bibliographic identifiers. -ISO 3166-1 Alpha-3 and Alpha-2: For country codes. -UN M.49 Codes: For regional (multi-country) codes. -ISO 639-1 and ISO 639-3: For language codes. -ISO 4217: For currency codes. Additionally, controlled vocabularies and taxonomies developed by the Land Portal include: -Themes and LandVoc Concepts: Based on Agrovoc, for classifying topical coverage. -Regions and Countries: For geographic classification. -Languages: For identifying resource languages. -Licenses: For copyright and licensing terms. -Land Library Resource Types: For bibliographic resource classification. -Organization Types: For classifying organizations. -Currencies: For specifying project budgets. Information Retrieval Land Portal partners utilize a variety of standards for data modeling and storage. These include: -AGRIS AP XML: For agricultural information management. -Open Archives Initiative Protocol for Metadata Harvesting (OAI-PMH): For metadata sharing. -Google Search Appliance Results: For indexing. -Journal of Economic Literature (JEL) Classification: For content tagging. -EndNote Library XML: For bibliographic data exchange. -RIS Format: For bibliographic citations. -Library of Congress Classification (LCC): For library categorization.

name: The Turing Way
description: The Turing Way is an open source, open collaboration and community-driven guide on data science. We involve an internal open science community in creating and sharing best practices for open, reproducible, ethical and collaborative data science.

sdgRelevance.04:
The Turing Way is relevant for SDG 4: Ensure inclusive and quality education for all and promote lifelong learning.

Particularly, The Turing Way contributes to the following two targets:

4.4.1 Target: "By 2030, substantially increase the number of youth and adults who have relevant skills, including technical and vocational skills, for employment, decent jobs, and entrepreneurship."
4.5.1 Target: “By 2030, eliminate gender disparities in education and ensure equal access to all levels of education and vocational training for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples, and children in vulnerable situations.”

The Turing Way is an open-source, collaborative, and community-driven project focused on data science and research reproducibility. The project encompasses a handbook in data science with five guides developed by a diverse community of contributors from various sectors. The Turing Way has been co-authored by more than 450 contributors from around the world and is utilized by a broad community of contributors, collaborators, and learners from academia, industry, and government.

Our community building and outreach practices are developed with specific goals to "increase the number of youth and adults who have relevant skills, including technical and vocational skills, for employment, decent jobs, and entrepreneurship” (SDG4- 4.4.1). Focusing on research, data science, and AI skills, we offer training, infrastructure, and opportunities for the community to get involved in shaping the narrative and direction of good practices.

Our community, with representation from both High and Low-to-Middle-Income countries, is dedicated to sharing and facilitating research best practices, tools, and real-world examples. The project is managed by the project delivery team, which includes two project leads, a research project manager, and a research community manager within The Alan Turing Institute's Tools, Practices, and Systems Research Programme. The governance body of The Turing Way is represented by the project leads and volunteer leaders who lead various formal and informal initiatives around shared goals. Particularly, both in practice as a community and in the recommendations (guides in The Turing Way book) for the broader data science ecosystem, The Turing Way stands as a strong advocate for “eliminating gender disparities in education and ensuring equal access to all levels of education and vocational training for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples, and children in vulnerable situations” (SDG4- 4.5.1).

name: The Ushahidi Platform
description: The Ushahidi Platform is an integrated data crowdsourcing and mapping tool that allows people to rapidly collect, manage and analyze crowdsourced information from their communities. Empowering communities to thrive as a result of accessible data and technology.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.05: SDG5: Harassmap. Born as a response to the persistent problem of sexual harassment on the streets of Egypt, to which society had become increasingly tolerant. It was the first independent initiative to work on this issue and was launched in December 2010 by a founding group of four women together with tech partners, advisers, and volunteers. It generated mass public dialogue, pushed the National Council for Women and several members of parliament to draft new laws, inspired a first successful court case, and encouraged women's NGOs who had previously been reluctant to take on this issue, to form an 18 member NGO Task Force on Sexual Harassment. In an independent review (https://www.ushahidi.com/in-action/towards-a-safer-city) of Harassmap.org, they concluded that the Ushahidi map is an effective tool for data collection for sensitive issues, encouraging more participation and sometimes more truthful reports than other typical data collection means. SDG6: Following the COVID pandemic, there was increased use of the Ushahidi platform globally by organizations and individuals self-organizing to provide mutual aid, document COVID-19 testing experiences, and create visibility on where to access essential resources for vulnerable communities. Ushahidi supported over 2000 deployments in over 140 countries. One such engagement was Humanitarian Open Street Maps (HOT) in Indonesia which set up a deployment to track and publicize handwashing stations across Indonesia to allow easier access for residents. The idea was inspired by early expert advice deeming handwashing as an effective way to prevent the spread of the virus. SDG13: Ushahidi was one of four organizations to win a Global Adaptation Index (GAIN) Prize in its inaugural year for its adaptation to urbanization, population growth, climate change, and other global challenges (https://www.ushahidi.com/about/blog/ushahidi-wins-global-adaptation-index-prize). One such climate change deployment is the Hatfield Climate Resilience-MVP Plan which crowdsourced information about Hatfield and its climate resilience (https://mvp.ushahidi.io/views/map). A second example is the Tana River Climate Change & Livelihoods Restoration Project (https://tclirp.ushahidi.io/views/map) by World Vision Kenya which aimed to contribute to enabling environmental policy implementation, governance, and environmental management through evidence generation using crowd geo-tagging. Case study report: https://www.gsma.com/mobilefordevelopment/resources/climate-change-adaptation-and-livelihood-restoration-in-tana-river-delta/?utm_source=LinkedIn&utm_medium=Social&utm_campaign=WVK SDG 16: On good governance, Ushahidi was born out of an electoral crisis in Kenya. Ushahidi in practice can be read in the published paper titled “Crowdsourcing Accountability in a Nigerian Election” in the Journal of Information Technology & Politics by Catie Snow Bailard & Steven Livingston, proving that the use of Ushahidi – ReclaimNaija (http://www.reclaimnaija.net/)- increased voter turnout in the 2011 Nigerian election by 8%). Additionally, Ushahidi has been used to monitor elections in India, Zambia, Mozambique, Nigeria, the USA, and many other countries over the past decade. Our strategy has evolved from primarily reactionary to proactively engaging with ordinary citizens and stakeholders to help foster transparency and accountability in elections. The United Nations (UN) has a long history of working to maintain peace and security around the world. It strives to improve relations among nations and protect human rights. A second use case of SDG 16 is The UN Department of Field Services which used the Ushahidi platform for its peacekeeping operations. Called SAGE—Situational Awareness Geospatial Enterprise—the UN used the Ushahidi platform to collect, process and disseminate information from their field staff so the mission HQ has a better understanding of what’s happening on the ground, can triage accordingly, and can make better decisions.

openAlternatives: An example is our SMS Sync product. We built it ground up, but some libraries have not been updated, and others have even been deprecated. However, it exists as a plug-in to the Ushahidi Platform, and Platform continues to operate normally without it. There also exists commercial + open-source alternatives such as Africa's Talking.

sdgRelevance.08: TradeTrust is an innovative framework with a targeted solution to address existing pain points in international trade (i.e., heavily paper-based and siloed systems, which lead to inefficiency) and support the growth of trade and income for all nations. It aims to connect the systems of governments and businesses with interoperable digital documents. It supports the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda because: 1. TradeTrust is a public good or digital infrastructure for the world. Its software code is made freely available on GitHub, reducing the barriers to entry for countries and businesses (i.e., promotes digital equality, especially for the less privileged). 2. It is about paperless trade and hence reducing the carbon footprint caused by paper documents used in the cross-border trade. 3. It promotes partnerships and inclusivity as it develops an open-source community and is open to collaborations with both public and private sector partners to showcase the benefits of digital trade. 4. Its various trials have demonstrated time and cost-saving for the business community (e.g., the Netherlands-Singapore trial proved time saving for BL transfer from 6-10 days to less than 24 hours). standardsAndPracticesNotes:
TYPO3's code adheres to a number of architectural and stylistic requirements and standards. The most important ones and how TYPO3 deals with them is described in detail at https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/CodingGuidelines/ The following list of standards support is not exhaustive: UTF-8 — https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/guide-frontendlocalization/main/en-us/CharacterSets/Index.html ISO-8859-1 ASCII HTML/XHTML CSS ES6 — https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/ApiOverview/Backend/JavaScript/ES6/Index.html JSON — input and output through the relevant implementations in the PHP programming language https://www.php.net/manual/en/book.json.php YAML — https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/Configuration/Yaml/YamlApi.html XML — input and output through the relevant implementations in the PHP programming language https://www.php.net/manual/en/refs.xml.php XLIFF — https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/ApiOverview/Localization/XliffFormat.html CSV HTTPS SSL PHP JWT PSRs 0, 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18 — https://www.php-fig.org/psr/ SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) PNG (Portable Network Graphics) JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group) Ogg MP3 (Moving Picture Experts Group: Audio Layer III) FLAC (Free Lossless Audio Codec) H.264 (H.264/MPEG-4 AVC) AAC (Advanced Audio Coding) MP4 (MPEG-4 Part 14) WebP AVIF WCAG 1.2

Change management using version control — https://github.com/TYPO3/typo3 Test driven development using automated tests — The TYPO3 core runs a large amount of unit, functional, and acceptance tests on all code contributions as well as around 200,000 nightly integration tests. https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/Testing/Index.html and https://git.typo3.org/typo3/CI/cms/-/pipelines Continous Integration & Continous Deployment (CI/CD) — TYPO3 installations supports CI/CD and the core makes heavy use of continuous integration during testing of code contributions and integration tests with new PHP and database versions. Code review — All code contributions requires code review and verification by at least two people. https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/guide-contributionworkflow/main/en-us/HandlingAPatch/Review.html#gerrit-policy-for-votes and https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/guide-contributionworkflow/main/en-us/CoreMergers/Review.html Code refactoring — Code refactoring happens regularly during core development. The TYPO3 Association has also financially supported the TYPO3 Rector and TYPO3 Fractor tools for easier refactoring of third-party code. https://github.com/sabbelasichon/typo3-rector and https://github.com/andreaswolf/fractor Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) organizes software design around data, or objects, rather than the functions and logic of procedural programming. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a collection of principles and patterns that help developers design elegant code around clearly defined conceptual models. Model-View-Controller (MVC) is a programming paradigm that leads to clear isolation of data, presentation layer, and business logic. Dependency Injection is a software design pattern that adds flexibility by removing the need for hard-coded dependencies. https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/ApiOverview/DependencyInjection/Index.html Separation of Concerns and Single-responsibility principle (SRP) are computer programming principles that help developers create modular, coherent, and maintainable software. Modularity and Extensibility — The TYPO3 core is split into 36 core extensions that implement different functionality within the CMS. Most of these extensions can be opted out of for individual instances of the software, depending on the user's wishes. TYPO3 also has a powerful extension API and many third-party extensions that implement additional functionality. It additionally supports the inclusion of third-party libraries through the Composer dependency manager. https://github.com/TYPO3/typo3/tree/main/typo3/sysext and https://extensions.typo3.org Maintainability and Predictability — TYPO3 has a very predictable release cycle, enabling long-term planning. Bugfix and security releases are published on a monthly basis and new major releases are published every 18 months. Each major release is supported with bugfix and security updates for up to 7 years. https://typo3.org/cms/roadmap Security — The CMS has detailed security guidelines and an active security team financed by the TYPO3 Association. The security team uses distributed security issue reporting and also manages security incident handling for third-party extensions. https://docs.typo3.org/m/typo3/reference-coreapi/main/en-us/Security/Index.html and https://typo3.org/community/teams/security

contentManagementPolicy:
As a content management system (CMS), TYPO3 allows logged-in editors to add content to pages on websites hosted on the solution through a backend interface.

As TYPO3 has to be installed by an external party (normally a web developer) on a third-party server, the moderation and detection processes are up to the external party on a case-by-case basis. Editor user accounts can only be created by assigned administrator users and the TYPO3 core features do not include the possibility for creation and publishing of content by other parties. TYPO3 also includes auditing functionality through the History module. This module allows administrators to see who and what content has been added within the content management system. Additional third-party extensions can be installed to automatically detect inappropriate and illegal content.

name: Uli
description: Uli is a browser plugin that provides tools for relief collective response to online gendered abuse. It is backed by open datasets of slurs and an ML model for redaction of gendered abuse in Indian languages.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.05: Uli as a plugin helps users tackle online gender-based violence on their browser feeds in India, which correlates to SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions). Further, the product is supported through annotations of slur words in multiple Indian languages by people belonging to marginalised genders and communities in India. The crowdsourced list of slurs is also publicly available for use by trust and safety teams to help them engage in better moderation practices. It also relates to SDG5 in as much as it supports women and marginalised genders by providing tools and resources for relief and building a collective response against online violence. Making online spaces safer for marginalised communities can advance other SDGs. Social media and other digital platforms are an extension of public spaces and are increasingly used to access essential services. Negative experiences online can reduce the safety and resilience of urban infrastructure, as well as the overall health and well-being of citizens. This became even more apparent during the COVID-19 pandemic, with communities relying on social media to mobilise resources, share critical health information, verify the availability of health infrastructure, and access public institutions (Wong et al. 2021). If silenced and removed from digital public spaces, marginalised groups are excluded from a range of essential functions accessed by users online.

dataPrivacySecurity:
Email: Uli has an archiving feature where archived posts are sent to an email. It also has a crowdsourcing feature; this feature needs a list of emails to which the Tweet link, on which action is requested, is sent. These emails as well as tweet links that are sent to the list of emails are stored on Tattle servers.

Uli only collects an email ID, and for the specific and limited purpose of sending archived posts/sending crowdsourced Tweet links. The user can reset the account, which will delete all the data on it within a month. Otherwise, this data is stored indefinitely for the purpose of ensuring Tweet links that the user requests action on are sent to the user as and when they flag it.
contentManagement: Content is collected and stored but NOT distributed.
contentManagementPolicy: Uli collects slur words in Indian languages for the purpose of filtering them out when the tool is active on a user's computer. It would/may qualify as the collection and storage of inappropriate content in this regard. The project moderates inappropriate/ abusive content online through redaction. This necessitates that we create and store a database of slurs and abusive content. We have a public dataset of slur words that we crowdsource from gender and feminist rights organisations. Activists and researchers identify the slur words and provide us with metadata through annotation exercises. This in turn helps the plugin filter slurs on a user's browser feeds. In all our datasets, personally identifiable information such as user handles are removed.

name: UrbanPy
description: A library to download, process and visualize high resolution urban data in an easy and fast way. It also estimates and visualizes urban service accessibility, i.e. how long it takes to reach a bank, grocery store, public park, hospital, etc., from every location in a city.

sdgRelevance.11: UrbanPy directly contributes to Target 11.1, "Safe and affordable housing", by solving the entire process of generating accessibility metrics, thus making it possible to quantify the lack of accessibility and pinpoint communities, particularly in informal settlements, with the most reduced access to essential urban services like public health, education, security and open/recreational spaces - this supports the 2030 goal to “ensure access for all to adequate, safe and affordable housing and basic services and upgrade slums.”. UrbanPy contributes to Target 11.2, "Affordable and sustainable transport systems", and specifically indicator 11.2.1 "Public transport access", as it can identify areas with low access to public transport and even estimate how many residents are affected. UrbanPy contributes to Target 11.3, "Inclusive and sustainable urbanization", particularly indicator 11.3.2 "Urban planning management" (proportion of cities with a direct participation structure of civil society in urban planning and management that operate regularly and democratically) by allowing anyone, any interested person, to easily produce updated diagnostics for their cities that show where investment should be prioritized improve access to essential urban services thus reducing inequality, improving quality of life, and bolstering sustainability. Diagnostics made with UrbanPy also contribute to Target 11.6, "Reduce the environmental impacts of cities", by informing decentralisation efforts -making sure everybody lives close to the places they need to visit in their daily lives- that can reduce pollution related to car-based mobility and longer travel distances. UrbanPy contributes to Target 11.7, "Provide access to safe and inclusive green and public spaces", by making it possible to diagnose accessibility to green spaces. As per above, UrbanPy supports Target 11.A, "Strong national and regional development planning", particularly the "ensure balanced territorial development" component of SDG Indicator 11.A.1 "Urban and regional planning".

name: Uwazi
description: Uwazi is an open-source web-based database application designed for human rights defenders to manage collections of information, including documents, evidence, cases and complaints.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.16:
Uwazi has enabled many organisations to bring more efficiency and rigour to their work - and show how documentation can advance impactful human rights work. It has proven to be a successful foundation for a range of different uses, such as monitoring and tracking violations for advocacy purposes, case management for use in litigation, collective memorialisation to serve longer-term justice efforts, and advance access to information, such as the creation of human rights digital information libraries.

We collaborate with local activist groups, national human rights institutions, large international NGOs and many organisations in between. Some of our partners specialise in specific issues such as arbitrary arrest, freedom of expression, women's and girls’ rights, reducing inequality, historical memory, and transitional justice, while others focus on human rights-related mechanisms such as the United Nations Human Rights Treaty System. Beyond their shared commitment to dignity and freedom, our partners have an important thing in common: they achieve greater impact when human rights-related information is easy to access, navigate and understand.

name: VaccineLedger
description: VaccineLedger is a decentralized supply chain management platform that leverages blockchain technology, Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Technology to capture data for every vaccine and other medical products in the supply chains from manufacturer to the beneficiary.

sdgRelevance.03: Nearly one million children die each year due to vaccine-preventable diseases. One of the major reasons for this is the lack of access to high-quality vaccines. Vaccine supply chains have a lot of existing issues such as cold-chain failures, expired products, and counterfeit products, and these failures have enormous costs associated with them. The platform ensures that the original product manufactured by the Manufacturer reaches the end beneficiary by identifying each unit as a unique digital ID and storing this information in a database so as to avoid any duplication and ensures end-to-end visibility and accountability, where different stakeholders can participate and collaborate over one single decentralized network. This makes VaccineLedger very easy to adopt and scale without having the need to replace existing systems and can easily integrate with them (SDG3 indicators: 3.b.1, 3.b.2) . Vaccine supply chains are complex and fragmented. Our goal is to innovate the supply chains, especially the Vaccine supply chain to have complete visibility and transparency across the various stakeholders, thus our platform VaccineLedger ensures all stakeholders have complete visibility of all vaccines and other life sciences products at different stages, using blockchain, and also predict and prevent failures in supply chains. (SDG9 indicators 9.5.1, 9.5.2) Vaccine delivery becomes more expensive due to wastage of vaccines, nearly 50%-60% of vaccines lose their efficacy because of cold-chain failures, however, supply-chain failures account for nearly 80% of the costs of the vaccines. VaccineLedger keeps track of all the batches and their expiry dates in order to prevent any usage of expired or counterfeit products, thus ensuring that the beneficiary receives certified products and if these losses are not prevented, then it becomes even more difficult to vaccinate people quickly and efficiently. (SDG12 indicators: 12.3.1 (a), 12.4.1)

nonPIINotes: This data is stored on Blockchain and can be accessible through REST APIs. The core idea of blockchain is collaboration based on shared data ownership, governance and operations. The major difference from centralized system architectures is that peers, collaborating in a network, can continue using their own systems and technology stack without the need to integrate them in the classical way. Instead, blockchain provides a shared data layer that allows these systems to interoperate on top and acts as the single truth. As a result, the network has no single authority, which owns the data or controls the systems. The decentralization of the ledger means a decentralization of power. name: Wikidata
description: Wikidata is Wikimedia's open community-curated knowledge graph. It acts as central storage for the structured data of its Wikimedia sister projects, including Wikipedia, Wikivoyage, Wiktionary, Wikisource, and others.

sdgs.name: SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.04: Wikidata ​contributes to many of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) ​w​ith its role as a multilingual collaborative knowledge base, serving as a central data source that supports applications and research by connecting information across languages and disciplines​. SDG 4: Quality Education: ​Wikidata makes information accessible in a machine-readable format that can be reused across languages, platforms, and educational tools. This enables students, teachers, and researchers to access, query, and connect knowledge globally, fostering inclusive learning, data literacy, and innovation in education. SDG 5: Gender Equality: Wikidata advances SDG 5 by enabling the collection and analysis of structured data on gender representation across fields, from politics to science. By making gender-disaggregated data freely available and linking it across languages, Wikidata helps highlight gaps, combat bias, and support initiatives that promote women’s visibility and equal participation in knowledge systems​. SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth: Wikidata contributes by offering free, structured data that supports research, innovation, and digital skills development. By enabling open access to information, it empowers entrepreneurs, developers, and policymakers to create tools and insights that foster sustainable growth, decent work opportunities, and a more inclusive global economy. SDG 9​: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure​: Wikidata drives SDG 9 by providing an open, structured data infrastructure that fuels innovation in research, technology, and education. Its interoperable knowledge graph supports digital tools, AI systems, and data-driven solutions, enabling industries, researchers, and innovators worldwide to build more inclusive, sustainable, and resilient knowledge infrastructures. SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities: Wikidata contributes to SDG 10 by offering open, structured data that can be accessed and reused globally, regardless of language or technical barriers. Its multilingual framework and machine-readable format help reduce knowledge inequalities by empowering marginalised communities, researchers, and developers to build inclusive tools and resources that bridge gaps in information access and representation​. SDG 16: Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions: Wikidata supports SDG 16 by providing transparent, verifiable, and openly licensed structured data that underpins evidence-based decision-making. By linking information across institutions, governments, and civil society, it fosters accountability, combats misinformation, and strengthens access to reliable data essential for peace, justice, and effective governance​.

We automatically receive the IP addresses of site visitors; these IP addresses are not publicly visible and are deleted, aggregated, or de-identified after 90 days at most. Wikidata doesn't require users to create accounts to read or edit. You can contribute anonymously without providing your name or email address. - Limited retention: Wikidata strives to minimize data retention. Non-public information, including IP addresses, is generally kept for a short time unless required for legal or security reasons. - Transparency: Wikidata has a clear privacy policy outlining its data practices and provides transparency reports about data requests from governments and other entities. - User control: Registered users have control over some of their data and can request deletion or anonymization in certain circumstances. name: Wikipedia
description: Wikipedia is a free online encyclopedia, created and edited by volunteers around the world and hosted by the Wikimedia Foundation.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.04: Wikipedia is relevant to many of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) due to its mission to provide free access to knowledge for everyone SDG 4: Quality Education: Wikipedia is a massive open educational resource that provides free access to information on a vast range of topics. This makes it an invaluable tool for students, teachers, and anyone seeking to learn. SDG 5: Gender Equality: Wikipedia is working to address gender bias on the platform by encouraging more women to contribute and ensuring that articles represent diverse perspectives. SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities: By providing free access to knowledge, Wikipedia helps to reduce inequalities in access to information. This is particularly important for people in developing countries and marginalized communities. SDG 16: Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions: Wikipedia promotes peace and justice by providing accurate and unbiased information on important issues. It also supports strong institutions by promoting transparency and accountability. SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals: Wikipedia is a collaborative platform that relies on partnerships with individuals, organizations, and institutions around the world to achieve its goals.

collectsPII: PII data is collected and stored and distributed.
dataPrivacySecurity:
IP addresses: We automatically receive the IP address of site visitors; these IP addresses are not publicly visible and are deleted, aggregated, or de-identified after 90 days at most. Consistent with our Privacy Policy (https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Privacy_policy#noaccount), when you edit without logging in, your IP address is recorded publicly for our volunteers to combat vandalism and spam.
Usernames and user contributions: If you create an account, your username and all your edits are publicly and permanently associated with it. This is essential for transparency and accountability.
Cookies: Like most websites, Wikipedia uses cookies for technical purposes like session management and user preferences.
Aggregated data: Wikipedia collects anonymized, aggregated data about usage patterns to analyze trends, improve the website, and for research purposes.

Wikipedia doesn't require users to create accounts to read or edit. You can contribute anonymously without providing your name or email address. Limited retention: Wikipedia strives to minimize data retention. Non-public information, including IP addresses, is generally kept for a short time unless required for legal or security reasons. Transparency: Wikipedia has a clear privacy policy outlining its data practices and provides transparency reports about data requests from governments and other entities. User control: Registered users have control over some of their data and can request deletion or anonymization in certain circumstances. otherAdoptingOrganizations: 1. International Governmental Organizations (IGOs): UN agencies (WHO, UNESCO, etc.): For research, background info, and potentially public outreach materials. Regional bodies (EU, ASEAN): May use it internally, and their websites might link to Wikipedia for general explanations of topics. 2. Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs): Advocacy groups (Amnesty, Greenpeace): For research, campaign material background, and potentially directing the public to info on their cause. Humanitarian aid (Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders): Potentially in disaster response for quick info on affected areas, languages spoken, etc. Development NGOs: Similar to IGOs, for research, understanding local contexts, and educational purposes. 3. name: Wikirate Data
description: Wikirate is an open data platform powered by a global community that collects, analyzes and shares data on company commitments, actions and impacts on people and the planet.

sdgRelevance.04: The Wikirate.org platform unites universities, civil society organizations, and students worldwide to gather, analyze, and share open data on how corporations influence and contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in relation to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) impacts. Participants in collaborative projects use public documents to record and input data on corporate sustainability performance across various topics and SDGs. The platform supports SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals) and SDG 4 (Quality Education, specifically Target 4.7: Education for Sustainable Development and Global Citizenship) by promoting collaboration, capacity building, and multi-stakeholder partnerships.

openAlternatives: WikiRate platform relies on some third-party proprietary services primarily for monitoring, analytics, data enrichment, and file processing capabilities (AWS S3, Google reCAPTCHA, Google Analytics, OAR ID API). The core application logic remains open source under GPL v3 license, but the integration with these proprietary services provides enhanced functionality for production deployments.

name: WSO2 Identity Server
description: WSO2 Identity Server is an open-source Identity and Access Management (IAM) solution supporting secure authentication, identity federation, and user management via open standards such as OAuth2, OpenID Connect, SAML, SCIM 2.0, and FIDO2.

sdgs.name: SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.09: SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure WSO2 IS provides essential digital infrastructure for secure access to government and industry services through standards-based authentication protocols (OAuth2, OpenID Connect, SAML, etc.). It facilitates innovation by enabling developers to build interoperable services using open identity standards, significantly reducing costs and complexity. Identity Server directly supports SDG targets: 9.1: Building resilient and sustainable digital infrastructure. 9.3: Enhancing small enterprises' access to digital financial services and integration into markets. 9.5: Promoting technological capabilities and innovation through accessible, standardized identity infrastructure. 9.c: Increasing universal, affordable access to ICT infrastructure. SDG 16: Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions By providing secure digital identities, WSO2 IS directly contributes to transparent, accountable, and effective governance. Digital identities reduce corruption, fraud, and bribery by creating transparent audit trails and ensuring accurate delivery of public services. It enables marginalized populations access to essential government services, enhances electoral processes, supports citizen engagement, improves inter-agency coordination, and strengthens border security and humanitarian responses. Directly supported targets include: 16.5: Reducing corruption and bribery. 16.6: Developing transparent and accountable institutions. 16.9: Providing legal identity for all. 16.10: Ensuring public access to information and protecting fundamental freedoms. SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals WSO2 IS promotes partnerships by establishing standardized digital identity frameworks that enable public-private collaborations across sectors such as finance, education, trade, and cross-border services. Its adherence to open standards fosters interoperability, enhances international cooperation, and supports regional integration. Directly supported targets include: 17.1: Strengthening domestic resource mobilization. 17.6: Enhancing international cooperation on technology and innovation. 17.17: Promoting effective public-private-civil society partnerships.

Typical data includes usernames, passwords (stored securely as salted hashes), first and last names, email addresses, mobile numbers, consent details, and other custom attributes as configured by system administrators. name: X-Road®
description: X-Road is open-source software and ecosystem solution that provides unified and secure data exchange between organisations.

sdgs.name: SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere
SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
SDG16: Peace¸ Justice and Strong Institutions

sdgRelevance.01:
In order to ensure more universal and affordable access to digital services for the population of developing countries, X-Road has been introduced in multiple projects around the world. X-Road is open-source software and it provides developing countries with a national data exchange infrastructure without licensing fees. By implementing X-Road, countries avoid a vendor lock-in situation and get multiple channels for support, including a global community of users.,

Different healthcare platforms can be connected securely with X-Road which enables data exchange between private and public service providers. All the evidence regarding the data exchange is stored locally by the data exchange parties, and no third parties have access to the data. Steps are being taken to introduce X-Road on a global basis, to allow either the World Health Organization (WHO) or its member states to set up various cross-border services to help the global community emerge faster from the COVID-19 health and economic crisis.,

Energy efficiency, renewables and consumer centricity figure among the lines of action to boost the transition towards cleaner energy systems – ways of producing, delivering and consuming energy in a more sustainable way. The deployment of information technology has a significant impact on the feasibility of contemporary policy actions. X-Road is helping electricity grid operators by harmonising access to energy data. By simplifying access to data lets them focus on the solutions to achieve energy and climate goals.,

X-Road enables reduction of administrative burdens by the implementation of the Once-Only Principle (TOOP). Streamlined administrative processes support economic growth and enable providing better services for the citizens. For example, in Estonia, X-Road saved 1,134 working years during the previous calendar year. X-Road helps a country to become a hassle-free environment for business and entrepreneurship, which also attracts foreign investments.,

X-Road provides national core digital infrastructure for data exchange between organizations across administration sectors and business domains. Typically, the ecosystem is open for all kinds of organizations – both public and private sector organizations. Besides, X-Road can be used to implement cross-border data exchange with other countries. X-Road enables allocating resources for building digital services and fostering innovation, instead of integrating services point-to-point.,

The use of digital services reduces the need to travel between different locations which reduces traffic in the cities. When travelling is needed, digital services provide information about different transportation and route alternatives and may prioritise the most environmentally friendly alternatives. X-Road is a crucial enabler that’s needed to make numerous information systems to communicate with each other. By establishing or joining an X-Road environment, cities and municipalities can request up-to-date information from relevant public registers and increase their effectiveness.,

The Nordic Institute for Interoperability Solutions (NIIS) aims to develop X-Road the most sustainable data exchange solution in the world. The short-term goal is to focus on the X- Road software's direct and tangible environmental impacts. NIIS conducted research focusing on assessing the current emissions profile across X-Road's operations and services to give targeted recommendations for emissions reduction and sustainable business practices.,

X-Road is a solution to fight against corruption and helps in building trust towards institutions. X-Road provides log records of each message sent between X-Road ecosystem member organisations. The log records provide undeniable evidence of a transaction, and they could be used in process automation to reduce manual work, increase the level of automation in various processes and make things easier for both users of different information systems and citizens. X-Road also provides many features that are required from MyData platform technology.

name: Xcapit
description: Xcapit is promoting financial inclusion by developing blockchain-based solutions that extend even to areas lacking digital infrastructure. This includes open-source, web 3 non-custodial crypto wallets and more.

sdgs.name: SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere
SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth

sdgRelevance.01:
SDG 1: No Poverty
Xcapit helps to mitigate poverty by providing financial tools that allow users to save in stronger currencies, safeguarding their wealth against local economic instability, such as inflation and currency devaluation. This capability is especially crucial for populations in regions like Latin America, where economic fluctuations can erode savings and perpetuate poverty.

SDG 5: Gender Equality
Xcapit promotes gender equality by empowering women through financial access. The platform's non-custodial crypto wallets enable women to have full control over their finances, fostering economic independence and decision-making power in a domain traditionally dominated by men.

SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
By facilitating quick and low-cost remittances, Xcapit supports economic growth and decent work. It provides a financial infrastructure that enhances the efficiency of money transfers, which is vital for migrant workers supporting families and investing back in their home countries.

SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure
The innovative use of blockchain technology by Xcapit contributes to building resilient infrastructure and promotes inclusive and sustainable industrialization. The open-source nature of Xcapit’s solutions also encourages wider participation in the development and refinement of these technologies.

SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities
Xcapit addresses economic inequalities by making financial services accessible to everyone, especially unbanked and vulnerable populations in developing countries. The platform ensures that all users, irrespective of their socio-economic background, have equitable access to financial tools and resources.

SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals
Xcapit’s commitment to open-source development fosters a collaborative environment for tackling financial exclusion. By partnering with developers, financial experts, and communities, Xcapit advances the implementation of these goals through collective expertise and shared objectives.

openAlternatives: All components are open source and a small number have hard dependencies. These components have been developed in a modular way and using interfaces that can be implemented to break the dependency. For example, we have used Firebase Remote Config, but we have developed it using interfaces that can be implemented so as not to depend on Firebase services.

name: Zamba
description: AI tools for wildlife monitoring with camera trap videos. Zamba is a command-line tool built in Python to automatically identify the species seen in camera trap videos from sites in central Africa. The tool makes predictions for 24 common species in these videos.

sdgRelevance.15: In line with target 15.5: "Protect biodiversity and natural habitats" & target 15.9: "Integrate ecosystem and biodiversity in governmental planning", camera traps are critical tools in research and conservation efforts because they allow ecologists, biologists, and other researchers to study valuable footage of wildlife without human interference. Still, camera traps can't yet automatically label the species they observe. It takes the valuable time of experts, or thousands of citizen scientists, to label this data. Zamba uses state-of-the-art computer vision and artificial intelligence to perform intensive camera trap video processing work, freeing up more time for humans to focus on interpreting the content and using the results.
